comments.name: osavus
comments.body: Who could blame republicans for staying home?  I didn't vote for trump but figured that he would be at least OK. Nope, I was wrong. trump will go down as the worst president of the USA.

comments.body: I love the anecdote of the one voter who thought Trump was NOW losing touch with the country but just wanted to go spend time with his dog... No reflection on his own part in this or his delusional state during the last election. Oops!

comments.name: Ben
comments.body: The MAGA movement will disappear the same way the No-Nothing Party did in the mid-1800s:  internal divisions, splits and election failures....and good riddance.  I am tired of the negativity and the chaos!

comments.name: Sue McCormack
comments.body: As I read the comments this morning I was struck by at least two things: The use of 'them' to describe Republicans and the MAGA group; and the overall denigration of people who voted for Trump and will continue to vote for him. I'm not happy at the smugness of those who say '...but didn't you recognize what a faker and con man he was when he came down the golden elevator'. People elect populists for a reason - they truly believe that one man or woman can make it all better. Can take away the pain of losing a job or watching inflation eat away at their future - just plain believing that they and their children have been left behind and that a rising tide really lifts all boats. We as a country have been torn by factionalism since our beginning. As I see it, political parties of any kind operate in their own best interests and only need the rest of us for our votes. However, I will vote on Nov. 3 but I also plan on sending letters to Democrats that you'd better not be the party of revenge - the low-hanging fruit are hearings, etc. I want you  to tell me how you are going to get legislative bodies to do their job as representatives of the people - all people. What's the plan to restore faith in facts and institutions. Frankly, we can't put the genie back on the bottle but we can build something better. I for one am disaffected with all the political class.

comments.name: Jim
comments.body:
A lot may swing on just how much distaste Republicans have for the Democrats. It's possible that will override any displeasure with Trump.

I've never had so much interest in the midterms in my whole life. Exciting!

comments.name: LL

Is this a matter of education or religion? It seems that the experience of Trump's first term would have been lesson enough. I feel grateful that all Michigan's statewide leaders are Democrats, showing that the people quoted are in the minority. Please keep Michigan's Senate seat blue!!!

We're done.   I look forward to the election day dance party.

I'm not pleased with Democrat legislators either, but they do by and large support the rule of law, and the separation of church and state, are far less racist and sexist.  I'll take that any day against a party that promotes a delusional felon whose main agenda seems to be enriching himself and his cronies. Unfortunately voters expect quick fixes and that's not going to happen.

Before you comment, sit and think about these statistics:
10,000+ rapes were REPORTED at American colleges and universities in 2024
Someone in the U.S. is sexually assaulted every 98 seconds.
Nearly half of all women experience contact sexual violence in their lifetimes.
Roughly 91% of rape and sexual assault victims are female, and 9% are male.

comments.name: TM
comments.body: This article begins to capture a very simple yet complex question, is there a situation where even if the person "consented", you should not move forward because the behavior and situation indicates this is not a healthy situation.  How many people want someone to cut off their healthy hand?  How many people want someone to hit them with a car?  How many people want somone to feed them strawberries non-stop for 3 straight hours?  Now assume the person asking is on drugs and/or super drunk.  In all these situations, we likely would decline to assist and would have some real questions about the cognitive state of the person, particularly if they were under the age of 25.  So why is it so hard to decide that it is not a healthy situation when a 20 year old who is both drunk and high claims they want to have simultaneous or consecutive sex with 7 people while others watch over a period of hours?  Just decline and get them to a safe space.

Consent isn't a good enough standard? Seriously? That sounds like pretty common language and an easily defined baseline to me. If there's any doubt at all about the other person's ability to consent, then there is no consent. 

This piece is the most bizarre mental gymnastics I've seen.

articles.title: Marco Rubio Gets to the Heart of the Matter
articles.summary: At the Acropolis, he says the West can revive itself by recalling its historic virtues and ambition.

comments.name: Robert Mutti
comments.body: Rhetoric has no political value unless it is believed and lived. Everybody whose eyes are open has seen Trump humiliate Rubio repeatedly, making it clear that there's nobody substantial behind this rhetoric.

comments.name: D E Kuppler
comments.body:
An honest Rubio wannabe adjusts his lapel, gazes at the Acropolis, & begins:

"Friends, Athenians, donors. Lend me your teleprompter. I stand before the Acropolis, that timeless symbol of Athenian democracy, & I promise to defend it in the same way my boss defends the rule of law: loudly, photogenically, and not at all. 

"Nothing says “Socratic inquiry” like a president who tried to overturn an election, defied court orders, pardoned insurrectionists, & installed his personal lawyers over the Justice Department. 

"Nothing says “fierce individuality” like abandoning every principle you once had to serve the con artist you used to warn us about. 

"Nothing says “daring exploration” like exploring how many international institutions we can abandon while treating allies like acquisition targets.

 "Nothing says “secrets of the cosmos” like the mystery of how the Journal can call this the speech of the year without laughing into its own editorial board. 

"To them, Western civilization is threatened by a college professor assigning a book on colonialism, but not by a president turning the executive branch into a private revenue stream. 

"The West they defend is curated pride & selective memory-airbrushed, amnesia-tested, &scrubbed of the enslaved people whose unpaid labor built the republic. 

"So let us raise a glass to Athens! Not the Athens of free thought &self-examination, but the Athens of marble backdrops & plausible deniability.

BELOW

comments.name: James
comments.body: A healthy public school system is the foundation of a healthy democracy. These billionaires know it which is why they attack it. We need to repeal the outrageous Citizens United ruling that has turned us into an oligarchy. These billionaires have WAY to much influence. Money is NOT speech - it is power, but not speech. I am sick of fighting with billionaires for the survival of my democracy. They need to be taxed properly and absolutely prevented from buying our governments. They should NOT have more voice than the average citizen.

comments.name: KT
comments.body: The history of voucher programs and charter school programs is deeply rooted in racism. After the landmark Brown Vs. Board of Education decision as schools were desegregated, parents and educators alike who did not want black students in their schools, started the vouchers and charter schools programs. Some of these were disguised as magnet schools, focused on a specific educational aspect, but underneath it all, it was and has always been about race. Now the discrimination is also directed towards poor children and children with disabilities. In a fair society, there will no charter school or a private school that is funded by public funds. They are and must be used for public schools.

comments.name: Allan S
comments.body: Everything in this column is maddening, but this sentence is the worst, and it's no one's fault but our own: "But the reason politicians don’t talk more about education is because voters don’t care about it." I guess if the best path to education reform is to rile people up over meddlesome billionaires, then fine, but I wish people would care about their local public school even without that hook.

comments.name: Grady
comments.body: I used to feel sympathy for people like the superintendent quoted at the beginning of this piece, but I have lost patience with those who consistently vote against their own interests, or to "own the libs". America needs significant re-education on media literacy, critical thinking, and empathy.

The miserable conditions in our public schools is connected to that decision. I am 77 years old. I have watched attacks on the schools and teachers throughout my life.  Given the white nationalist agenda I cannot see an end to this madness.

comments.name: Robert McConnell
comments.body: First of all, our military is not simply an offensive weapon. It is equally, a weapon of deterrence. Relying solely on a military of draftees is way too slow to respond to international threats in today's world. And the complexity of modern warfare, offensive and defensive, requires years of training. Impossible in a draft only military.

comments.name: Ron Prichard
comments.body: The military Pete seems to be building is more interested in beach muscles than real muscles, so to speak, as he talks tough but retreats globally in the face of Iran (as the Times documents today.) He readies troops for fistfights but not for drone warfare or missile defense, which takes techies rather than bodybuilders.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
French: "[B]efore I went into journalism, I served in the U.S. Army. I was a judge advocate general officer, an Army lawyer. I deployed to Iraq in 2007 ... So I can say from some degree of experience that I’m worried about the way Pete Hegseth, the secretary of defense, is managing the war in Iran.

As a lawyer, your first worry should be how Trump was allowed to start a war with Iran without the congressional approval required by the U.S. Constitution.

And Hegseth is rightly calling himself secretary of war.

comments.name: MSL
comments.body: I was a USAF intelligence analyst for 10 years, during and after the Vietnam war. Our job was to locate and identify enemy targets for destruction from the air. In terms of “lethality”, I can assure Hegseth that the work that we did resulted in immensely more enemy casualties than all of the Special Forces troops in SEA combined. None of us aspired to look like GI Joe. We were selected for our ability to competently do the job, not because we looked like we were models for a recruiting poster. The current drive towards a legion of tough guy, push-up contest winners populating our military relies on small brains. A better approach (as seen in Ukraine) is fielding forces with bigger brains and fewer physical fitness awards. This will only become more obvious as the population of the United States grows increasingly averse to their leaders cavalierly committing ground troops on a whim and then watching their sons and daughters come home in metal boxes. Welcome to the coming age of drones and asymmetric warfare- no more D-Days, no more Iwo Jimas, no more Okinawas.

comments.name: gern blansten
comments.body:
The things that concern me are (a) parading his religion, perhaps even integrating it into our forces (crusade, anyone?) and (b) the disdain he displays for the average citizen, who our forces’ mission is to protect and defend.

This fox state tv attitude of disrespect for anyone who doesn’t agree with you, has been corroding our society for a long time.

comments.name: JohnnyC
comments.body: I believe that all of Trump’s actions should be examined in light of his alliance with and subservience to Putin. So how does the Iran war look in that light?  The misadventure with Iran has resulted in a great degradation of U.S. military capabilities and impairs our ability to provide support to Ukraine. Trump has also used the Iran war to claim, falsely, that our NATO allies owed us their support in the war and that they have failed us, thereby adding weight to his argument that the alliance does not benefit the U.S., and increasing the concern that Europeans should not count on U.S. support if Putin more directly attacks a NATO ally. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz puts far greater economic strain on our historical European allies who actively oppose Putin’s ongoing war on Ukraine than it does on the U.S. Trump’s failed Iran war is a big victory for Putin. In that light, the failed Iran war is a victory for Trump.

comments.name: John
comments.body: I find it interesting that in the discussion of the war in Iraq much is made of the Bush administration's efforts to sell the war to the public and to Congress and of Bush's "right" decision about the surge while completely ignoring the lies the war was based on (WMDs anyone?) and further ignores the trillions of dollars wasted in pursuing that war and the follow-on war in Afghanistan.  There may be goals that would be worth that level of financial destruction (to say nothing of the lives lost and bodies traumatized) of the USA, but certainly nothing in the Middle East justifies it.

comments.name: vis gh
comments.body:
What we can’t fix through fiscal discipline, will get fixed for us through inflation.

I hope we buried the Modern Monetary Theory in the ocean.

There are consequences to printing money!

comments.name: James Bach
comments.body: Inflation since Covid has been a huge hurdle.  First it was Trump and the GOP that gave away trillions.  Then Biden and the Democrats wanted their turn at the sweepstakes giveaway.  Coupled with deficit spending through Obama, Trump, Biden, then Trump again the national debt has ballooned to $40 trillion and climbing.  Interest rates on that debt have mushroomed because the world has a debt problem.  This will only get worse because politicians of all stripes simply won’t stop spending.

comments.name: Gary Bubis
comments.body: Simple economics.  Inflation is here to stay regardless or the party in power.   "WE" have to inflate our way out of the never ending debt obligations.  Anyone using their protest vote thinking that inflation will stop lives on another planet.

comments.name: John Herbert
comments.body: Tax relief has helped those at the top, but the money doesn't trickle down, never has, never will.

comments.name: petey b
comments.body: This article is a mishmash of different chart types:  derivative of price,  price/(value at start date), absolute price.  But fortunately there is one graph that simply compares trend in prices vs wages.  And from that chart we can glean that the only costs that are going up faster than wages are car repair and pet services. This is why people's hair is so on fire about "affordability."

comments.name: Ethan D
comments.body: Both parties are focusing on prices in their campaign messaging. Really? It seems like all the Republican campaign ads are laser focused on preventing boys from playing in girls sports.

comments.name: Ray L
comments.body: There are different types of inflation which is why no one solution fits all.  However one type of inflation can be remedied much sooner.  Trump's tariffs result in Cost Push Inflation.  Tariffs increase the cost of imported goods as well as goods made with imported parts without any corresponding increase in value of the product.  If all tariffs were cancelled today, many companies would roll back prices.  We'll need to have a Consumer Watchdog to advertise the companies gaming the tariff cut by keeping the money but some may change with appropriate consumer pressure.

comments.name: Thomas Nicolay
comments.body: Excellent article Owen. The Michigan consumer sentiment index has been in the relative basement for years, given the accumulation of inflation over time. Of course, none of the declining short term metrics will undue the damage that's been done to the Main Street economy. The problem, as Warsh correctly points out over the past few months, sits squarely with the Fed, a Fed that until June of this year continued to add inflation-inducing liquidity via the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's federal open market operations, at a time of 5 years of above target inflation. Clearly, the Fed for years and years created way too much credit and therefore too much inflation over time.

comments.name: Ouzo
comments.body: Don't know the original source of this one, but I think it is maybe appropriate here: "Never argue with a man whose job depends on not being convinced."

comments.name: Eastsider
comments.body:
This isn't about Tech, this is about political attitude. Left vs. Right.

While I agree that hardware isn't the problem, it's the software. I also believe the dangers are way overblown. Sure, Bill Gates is concerned, he is a derivative thinker who started a company that simply bought or borrowed from all its competitors.

Like any new technology, there will be evolving problems and solutions.  Hacking and cybersecurity have been internet problems from day one. Has that stuffed anyone from using the internet? No.

The real issue, politically speaking is, who is for and who was against AI? The more progressive and the more left, the more you hate it, the more centrist, and somewhat right, the more you embrace it.

So you might as well ask the question, what's really going to end the world as we know it, the Democrats or the Republicans?

comments.name: JC
comments.body: I am a long term NVDIA investor and have always admired the technical prowess of this company and, of course, its massive growth. All of that changed when I listened to Ezra Klein's interview with him a couple of weeks ago. He came across as arrogant and defensive. He talked over, interrupted, and appeared to lack the ability to reflect on ideas inconsistent with his own self interest. More importantly, his position was exactly what you would expect from someone whose company profits from the unregulated growth of AI. I am constantly amazed by this technology and I see it benefiting mankind IF it is regulated. On another note I'm surprised Huang waded into this mess - he has been diminished by it.

comments.name: Minitoaster
comments.body: The irony is the irony that this article points out: while the software developers magnify the power of their product by instilling it in almost godlike terms, Mr. Hong is exposed to a bias of having unending production of AI and data centers in order to keep his company profitable. There has to be a constant push to accept AI in order for Nvidia to remain the most profitable company in the world. How are we supposed to judge when both the doomsayers and the optimists have economic incentive to take their positions?

comments.name: Dennis M.
comments.body:
When the only tool you have is a hammer, every problem begins to look like a nail.

The last think we need is a "chief engineer" who thinks he can fix everything. When you "jump to a solution" without carefully considering the real underlying problems, things may continue to get worse (even after spending trillions).

We know that there are problems that do not have a simple engineering solution. We know that some attempts to solve big problems at a global level will create a lot of small problems at a local level.

comments.name: Ralph Smathers
comments.body:
It is false to say that the artificial neurons of current AI machines are perfectly predictable.  The very nature of neurons, real and artificial, involves randomness.  Possible outputs have probabilities assigned but which possible output is selected is based on that probability, there is no certainty which output will be selected.

That unpredictability is part of the software, it is not hardware based with GPU based machines which may explain why hardware engineers don't see a problem that software engineers do.

To the hardware engineer the machine just sits there running black box software.  To the software engineer they know that black box has a network connection and is capable of doing anything possible over a network.

comments.name: Eben Spinoza
comments.body: I'm way less worried about the technology than the people who own it and the economics that it can unleash.  Theoretically, a world in which robots can do all the work could be a paradise. But if all of the "value" of the productivity accrues to the nominal owners, we're sunk as a society.   What's going on right now is that the knowledge of the world is being collected for little or nothing from it sources, then refined and sold back to them at vastly higher prices.  The feudal Lords are enclosing the common lands.

articles.title: He’s the Most Powerful Engineer on Earth. Here’s Why He Thinks A.I. Is Going Great.
articles.summary: Our fate may be very well be in the hands of Jensen Huang.

comments.name: ThatGuy
comments.body:
“I don’t think that alignment is an engineering problem. I think it’s a science problem. It’s not that we haven’t got the resources or we’re not trying hard enough — we don’t know how. That’s what the problem is with alignment.”

Well, with Global Warming we DO have the science as well as the engineering. And we've had LOTS of time to make corrections to a slow moving change. And thanks to greed we have UTTERLY failed. There is nothing on the horizon to suggest AI will end otherwise. 

However, if the machines are actually smarter than us and even a teenie bit wiser, I don't see human extinction as a good strategy. Machines are a long way from being able to automate chip manufacturer, even if they have better designs. More likely. I think, is that humanity will be subtly controlled and contained.

comments.name: gs
comments.body:
The analogy with safety regulation in nuclear and aviation (and pharmaceuticals) is not entirely reassuring.
Nuclear accidents have taken place 1000 times more frequently than originally predicted by the experts, so it is not surprising that the industry (at least in the US and Germany) has been regulated to death. Moreover, nuclear, in contrast to solar and wind, has not demonstrated any learning economies, i.e., becoming cheaper with use.
And even the success story of aviation did not prevent two Boeing 737 MAXs from crashing due to inadequate design by Boeing and inadequate regulation by the FAA.
An “AI“ crash may be much more consequential, as it might bring down the entire Internet or the financial and health systems, or launch a war.
A reassuring lesson of nuclear may be that (particularly proprietary) AI may simply be too expensive to establish itself longterm in the economy. At the moment it is running on bubble fumes.

comments.name: Peter L
comments.body: The AI companies seem puzzled by the fact that their products don't always do as the companies would wish.  But aren't the products taught from material that covers a wide array of behaviours, including disobedience and prevarication?

comments.name: Elizabeth
comments.body:
Ezra, fantastic interview! Thanks for this deep dive.

One thought - I wonder if biological research might be an interesting metaphor for AI research, in that engineering one or many "super bugs" that may be more than humans can retain dominion over, and the thing being grown carries a lot of risk. Containment. Controlled capacity.

comments.name: Therese
comments.body:
Incredible article!  Thank you for putting this together.  As you both said “This is crazy!” 
And it’s just the beginning.  I have very little faith that much good will come from the trajectory we are on, especially as this will take worldwide cooperation to slow the “frontier” or insure alignment of AI.  Humans do not seem capable of working together.

comments.name: dans
comments.body: I am shocked that we have not heard from internet security experts concerning worst case scenarios of how AI could breach the security or firewalls of the myriad of ecommerce, banking, industrial production control, utility control and financial transaction software on the internet. This to me is the biggest threat of the software.

comments.name: Kbu
comments.body:
All these interviews of lack of safety and catastrophic consequences are invaluable but..

The public, every commentator and politician should be demanding Hearings to ask all these tech-AI  leaders to appear before them and ask them a few simple questions - not about the good and bad of AI. 

But the questions should be (and the answers simple): what is your end game? What kind of physical world do you envision for all of mankind.  
Do you yourself believe in Democracy? 
Do you see that AI could destroy democracy? 
Do you believe, as the likes of Musk, Altman, Peter Thiel etc have said in public, that the world would be better for EVERYONE, if there was one Benevolent Dictator who would alleviate regulations and laws to ensure tech advancements. 

Musk said outside the White House with Trump and tech bros surrounding him, in response to being asked, "-should we fear mass unemployment?"  Musk said, "AI will bring us to a new level of high wealth abundance for everyone.And working-employment will look different in this new world."  

So these tech bros see that everyone is going to have abundant wealth, not a few, everyone.

This is absurd, because if there is little or no human employment, Musk (DOGE chainsaw guy!), where/how does the capitalist society function?

These are the questions that need to be asked because the tech guys see themselves as saviors and we are disposable in the self-righteous quest.

Simple questions need simple answers, before its too late.

comments.name: ELin
comments.body: Every time I have used AI, it has lied, deceived or manipulated. How can I possibly have faith in ANY OF IT??? Explain THAT to me. Because if I had an employee who did that, they would be fired. So, I'm supposed to be excited by swarms of AI agents who we can't trust, who will do all those things - and I'm just supposed to give over my power to them/that? It makes me so angry. But heaven forbid I have any EMOTION about it. Because that's so HUMAN. How do people not understand - we will be RUINED by it? And I have tried to see the positive, the "utopia". But there's no point in having a cure for cancer when you've surrendered all autonomy, human-ness, and you've destroyed the world.

articles.title: ‘This Is Nuts.’ An OpenAI Insider Explains Why He Quit.
articles.summary: David Robinson, who wrote OpenAI’s safety protocols, resigned last week over safety concerns.

comments.name: Sophia
comments.body: After the Oct 7 attack and the ensuing decimation of Gaza, I began wearing a bracelet made of olive wood, to remind me of the horrible actions of human beings and the suffering it brings. The bracelet hasn’t fallen off yet; there’s apparently more work to do on both sides.

comments.name: jody
comments.body: I was privileged to hear the stories of some of the survivors of Kfir Azar and my heart aches for the trauma and terror Israelis endured that day and everyday since. On October 6 there was relative peace in the middle east.  Today, there is horror upon horrors. Whatever the goal of Hamas, they failed miserably.

comments.name: Jean F.
comments.body: As the mother of twin sons about the same age, I wish these young men healing in their journey to recover from this ordeal.  However,  I can not forget the people of Gaza and the West Bank who have also suffered starvation, bombardment, and the loss of their land.  Real peace is needed in Israel, Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon to break this cycle of extreme violence and dehumanizing one another.  Other countries in sustained and bloody conflicts have been able to achieve peaceful coexistence through dialog.  I encourage leadership in this conflict to summon the courage to seek a resolution for this never ending war. In addition,  those who reject dialog and sustain continued conflict must be rejected.

comments.name: Stephanie
comments.body:
Ziv and Gali Berman are home, released by Hamas. Their return is a reminder that no civilian should be held for someone else's war.

That principle has to apply to everyone. Borak and Hashem Alagha, American citizens from the Chicago area, remain in Israeli custody. If we celebrated the Bermans' release, we cannot be silent about the Alaghas. Humanism does not ask whose neighbor, government, or captor was responsible before it asks for a person's freedom.

The terror of October 7 and the devastation visited on Gaza afterward are both anti-humanist, because both treat human beings as expendable. 

A ceasefire has existed on paper since October 2025, yet strikes continue, Hamas has not disarmed, Israeli forces control far more of Gaza than the plan envisioned, and the vast majority of Gazans still live in tents or ruins. Reconstruction funding falls far short of the need. The machinery that feeds this violence has to be halted, not paused.

So I call on readers, and on this paper, to hold one standard for every civilian:

- Israel and Hamas should honor the ceasefire in full, and Hamas must disarm.

- Israel should release the Alagha brothers.

- Reconstruction should begin without delay, with Palestinians themselves at the table.

- Withdrawal commitments should be kept, and civilians who wish to leave Gaza should have safe passage.

Mourning one family's suffering should never require ignoring another's. We can hold both, and we must.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body:
Feel sorry for citizens of both Israel and Palestine however a democracy should have rounded up the perpetrators and brought them to justice, Israel had them locked up in Gaza so they where not going anywhere however they didn't, no inquiry into how Hamas breached Israel and stayed there for hours is suspect as I wouldn't trust netanyahu and his right wing government.
The war got trump over the line against Biden as all Muslims went well Republicans and we know Iran china and Russia wanted trump elected. It was probably going to happen in any ways however Iran timed it wiell for the American election

comments.name: Denise
comments.body: It's unimaginable what these brothers went through. What a blessing that they survived their ordeal and that their parents and brother did as well. So many people did not have that outcome on either side of this war, but it warms my heart that they did. I hope Gali and Ziv and their family can all move forward together, bolstered by the tremendous love and support they have for one another. Fanatical and callous leaders continue to wage war but it's always innocent civilians who suffer from their terrible and inhumane choices.

comments.name: sojourner treuth
comments.body: Those who are completely critical of Israel fail to acknowledge that Hamas was the government of Gaza, and the army of that government invaded a sovereign nation.  It purposefully attacked and killed its civilian citizens.  That is an act of war.  The government of Israel responded with a war in return to Gaza.  The fact that Hamas hid its fighters and weapons among civilians accounts for the high casualty numbers, including the fact that Hamas never distinguished among civilian and fighter casualties.  That is not to say that in some cases Israel may have responded harshly, but war crimes are often committed in total war, even by the USA.

articles.summary: Gali and Ziv Berman were taken hostage when their kibbutz was attacked on Oct. 7, 2023. They were freed a year ago but are still adjusting to freedom and trying to rebuild their lives.

comments.name: Pamela
comments.body: Yikes. Did "Uncle" even reread his letter before sending? Low on manners, low on impulse control (as noted), and most of all, a jerk to his sister on a day that was meant to celebrate her. He owes his sister a big apology.

comments.name: Fomo brood
comments.body: I understand the niece quite well. I was in hospitality for decades.  Some people like the LW think the world of themselves.  LW had the whole evening to catch up with yje friend.  The niece was eager to get the party started. Food  can get cold or too warm or melts are too well done. The  party was  for her mom not you. U should be the older and wiser one and not a rude hothead. Did you apologize to your sister?  You think your money is so important??? I know your type and dont care for your type at all.

comments.name: Ellen Jones
comments.body: Letter #3 - the female relatives flew in for the bridal shower - presumably they gave a gift at that juncture, that's what showers are all about - if they are not attending the wedding, you're annoyed that they didn't send a second gift?

comments.name: Anne P.
comments.body: My brother and i fought physically and repeatedly when we were chldren.  It came to a stop one day and forever when i was 9 and he was 8 and he shoved me so hard my elbow went through the dining room window.  Thankfully for both of us the heavy drapes protected me from cuts or lacerations.  Without a word we somehow both recognized that he was now stronger than i was and we never fought again (physically, that is 🙂).

comments.name: Nula
comments.body:
We get it that niece was trying to organize and help get things going. She may also have been on the receiving end of a harsh tongue earlier.  While her behaviour was rude and wholly inappropriate ( for any age), LW's wasn't so hot either. 
 There are many ways in which he could have dealt with her tone and her command : ie: "Niece; I will sit down in just a moment, I am finishing up here with Joe." . Even joking a little: "Niece: let's do a retake of this scene, please.---'Uncle, we are starting the festivities, it is time to be seated.' "Then pretend to use  film clapper. Said in the appropriate tone of voice, such phrases let her know she was totally out of line, but model better behaviour. 
The one thing left out is the apology to the party he was conversing with.

comments.name: Michelle
comments.body:
Re: wedding gifts, my husband and I received some gifts nearly a year after the ceremony. So don’t assume no gift is ever forthcoming.That said, no one is obliged to give a gift…that’s why they are called gifts, and not, say, “tributes”. 

We waited a while to send thank you notes, and then sent them to everyone. The handful of guests that didn’t bring a gift got a “thank you for being there to celebrate with us” message. And we meant it!

Perhaps you could send him a few photos and a message along the lines of “we missed you and wish you could have been here to celebrate with us.” It may stimulate a congratulatory card or gift. If not, let it go.

comments.name: Margie
comments.body:
Re: My Rude Niece:  LW, I  understand you felt your niece was rude in asking your to come over and be seated, when you were not ready to sit down and begin a birthday luncheon.   Things escalated into you both yelling rude words at each other.  You both were in the wrong: She should not have yelled at you, and YOU should not have yelled at her.  YOU were wrong in not going to table; you were holding up the lunch!  People were waiting on you, and instead of coming to sit down ya'll gave them a show!   LW, both of you were in the wrong here.

  You don't have to leave this lady  an inheritance, but don't use this as an excuse.  You should, however apologize to your sister  for putting on a show at her birthday party.   Her daughter owes her one too.

comments.name: We have lost our way as a country
comments.location: Lisbon by way of the US
comments.body:
The word of the day in these two letters: ENTITLEMENT!

I am so glad that I don't have toxic people in my life (except those running the country right now). A gift, a request to sit down...all while our world is on fire right now....talk about being self involved!

articles.summary: A reader was stunned when his adult niece brusquely ordered him to take his seat at a brunch — so much so that he resolved to write her out of his will.

comments.name: Buff Orpington
comments.body:
Twilight Zone the Movie from 1983 was a disappointment.
There was one good episode though, It’s a Good Life.

Billy Mummy, who played “ wish him into the cornfield” Anthony on the original tv episode is one of the young men playing pinball in the brief diner scene, which was a nice touch I thought.

comments.name: Steve Paradis
comments.body:
You had to have grown up in the CONELRAD era, when all large buildings had their fallout shelters spaces signposted, H-bomb tests were on the nightly news and PSAs were of the duck-and- -cover variety to appreciate "The Shelter".
A well-liked but slightly eccentric doctor builds a personal fallout shelter in his backyard. It's a local joke . . .  until the sirens sound and everyone wants to get in it.

comments.name: Puny Earthling
comments.body: We need to wish Donald Trump into the corn field.

comments.name: Mark Siegel
comments.body: I watched this great show as a kid and still do on SyFy. The stories are exceptionally well written and thoughtful.  I can only imagine how Serling would do an episode about a lying, narcissistic, corrupt dictator who routinely flouts the law and starts wars for no good reason.   How would he do that without naming you-know-who?

comments.name: bl
comments.body:
We will always remain immobilized in a cocoon of self and media induced ignorance until it is too late to do anything constructive to save us. 

This society has so many structural failures,  deep distrust and cynical contempt for the other,  a political system that is drowning in corruption, ineptness, moral cowardice, and posturing, social media sites  that are committed more to disinforming and manipulating for the sake of profit than genuine informing for the sake of the public good, that there is no evident corrective agent(s) that can perturb the society off  its rendezvous with doom. 

The evidence is all around to mull over. 

Take the Senate race in TX. A thoroughly contemptible and morally corrupt individual is in the process of buying his Senate seat with huge amounts of anonymous media buys, and is offering no vision of anything other than more of the trumpican same old same of identify, lie, and attack in the name of American greatness. How is it possible that he is almost neck and neck with his opponent, someone diametrically opposite in decency  and commitment to the common good?

How can it be that millions of Texans are not thoroughly revolted by paxton's decision to investigate the state's pediatricians because he "suspects" that they've made medical judgements to benefit vaccine makers and not  their patients? What deluded  mindset could possibly think such idiocy justifies a Senate seat? 

Are there really not enough texan voters capable of moral clarity?

comments.name: Jim P
comments.body: Twilight Zone and Outer Limits were two of my favorite Tv shows. However I think Rod Serling’s best work was his adapted screenplay for “Seven Days in May”.  I wonder if Sect. Of War Pete Hegseth ever watched it?

comments.name: LLM
comments.body: In the 1960s, "That Was The Week That Was," or TW3 was a funny satirical look at politicians, ways, assumptions, arrogance.  We need that now, even more than then. (And yes, a Boomer here, and oh did you young ones miss a lot that we would feast upon.)

comments.name: Russell Potter
comments.body: Oh, where to begin with Serling's prescience? I'd start with "It's a Good Life," where Billy Mumy portrays a child tyrant with absolute power, such that whatever he does, all the adults simply say "that's good ... that's real good" -- there's Trump in a nutshell. And let's not forget "Night Gallery," which in many ways further concentrated the Serling serum -- I'll always remember Elsa Lancaster (erstwhile Bride of Frankenstein) in "Green Fingers," when she plants her own fingers and grows to wreak revenge against a greedy developer. I think the problem with shows today that try to echo Serling's mastery is that they are too timid, too afraid to take a tale to its ultimate limit. And since that's where we find ourselves today, Serling's way is more timely than ever.

Hubby

comments.name: Seely Pratt

comments.name: Rico Bartolo

This problem cannot be solved solely with technology!

Consult with Israelis -- no commercial Israeli flight has ever been deliberately crashed due to terrorism. El Al, is widely recognized for having some of the most stringent aviation security protocols in the world, which has successfully prevented any catastrophic crashes resulting from terrorist acts...

comments.name: Mike Hosking
comments.body: Autonomous airliners are the future, no matter how much pilots unions will fight them (as they did two man crews).  Incidents like this will help to rally public support for autonomous aircraft.  Its not going to happen right away, but id be shocked if the first flight is more than 2 decades away.  In the meantime stick with major carriers and preferably domestic carriers. Avoid any carrier who embraces DEI as it is a sign they will ignore inconvenient facts like the potential for radicalization.

comments.name: Joseph Giardino
comments.body:
Nothing is funnier to me than seeing and hearing people exclaiming, with great exuberance, how they ‘broke’ their ‘Digital Addiction!”
Even funnier is how, now that they are ‘free,’ they become “Anti-phone Evangelists” and hope to ‘spread the word’ about their new-found freedom and want us to follow!
I always wondered how it’s possible how they got hooked in the first place. Did someone pass a law saying they MUST sign up for Snapchat FaceBook, Instagram, Twitter/X? Did this law also demand they Must comment on a picture of someone’s lunch, weigh in on every topic under the sun, and have to see the latest trending TikTok videos?
Some of us naturally do not get dragged into compulsively posting and commenting on all Social Media channels. Having a cell phone, since 1993, and a smart phone since 2010, I see it as a useful tool, and once it went ‘smart’ it became a very useful tool! But addiction? Really?
So many armchair sociologists telling us how lost we have become because we have become “zombies,” with our heads buried in our phones. Nonsense! Before the smart phone, all we could do was daydreamed! That was it!! At least with a smart phone, our minds are ACTIVE! When I’m waiting for the bus, I can catch up with the news, family communications, weather, make lists, look up events on the web. Hardly qualifies ‘making us zombies.’
If some feel like they are addicted, well, more power to them for breaking it, but to think everyone ELSE has the same problem, guess again!

comments.name: Gia
comments.body: I'm sure she means well, but I'm personally sick of people proselytizing to me to reject (name a modern trend or technology) to embrace a time I already lived through. A phone-less, internet-less, social-media-less existance was fine, but times have changed. It seems to be an involuntary tick for the younger generation: I decided to change my life in a certain way, and now I think everyone else should too! It's just an IRL version of all those TikTok and IG reels. No one person has THE ANSWER for everyone else. They just have the answer for themselves.

comments.name: PG
comments.body: She's on to something. I definitely spend way too much time on the stupid phone and some days wish I would throw it into a lake. At the same time, it's incredible technology, and you can't attend a sporting event or do many other things without one. Seeing that "screen time" figure really hurts, I can't even look at it. Just the amount of time spent on it, much of it not productively, is scary and sad. And I'm not even on social media.

comments.name: Hyla
comments.body: I think the TobiPhone solves this. An iPhone but with none of the addictive junk on it and no workarounds.

comments.name: Pittsburgh Mike
comments.body:
Just delete your social media apps, YouTube and Tik Tok and you'll still be able to use your phone to hold boarding passes and credit cards, but you won't get sucked into the void.

Basically get rid of anything that lets you do infinite scrolls.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body: She's hustling a book.

comments.name: Kermit Myers
comments.body: Bring back "The Talking" Yellow Pages. Few may remember that you could call, for free, numbers found within the Yellow Pages print directory and get information on the days weather, movie showtimes, even your horoscope. Big Tech has already destroyed so much and we desperately need alternatives to the failing systems they have made us all reliant upon before the house of cards they have built comes tumbling down.

comments.name: Tim
comments.body: If you think switching from a smart phone to a flip phone makes you a Luddite, I don't really know what to say to that. You should try spending a month or two with no phone at all and see just how free you can be when you're not at anyone's beck and call.

articles.summary: August Lamm was an Instagram artist with a robust following. Now she believes we should put down our smartphones and reclaim our lives.

comments.name: Thomas

comments.name: Fiona

comments.name: Max Davies
comments.body:
I like some aspects of Originalism because they apply a brake to runaway judicial rulings that originate in the culture and prejudices of judges.

But Originalism should be seen as having two layers. The first, and overarching one, refers to the principles rather than the details of how people can be forced to submit to the will of the State. These principles are both stated in plain English and strongly implied by the debates when the Constitution was written and amended, especially by the Bill of Rights.

The second layer, beneath the first and subservient to it, finds the detailed implementations of these principles. Here is where Originalism provides an interesting perspective and a caution to slow down, but not a satisfactory framework for legal rulings.

I accuse Originalists of not seeing the distinction between the layers, of applying their philosophy in a facile way that could allow, in the suggested example, states to flog their citizens and go against the absolute limitation on their power explicit in the first layer.

comments.name: Mr. Jones
comments.body: We can never know why any particular justice adheres to the ideas of “Originalists”. Their adherence might reflect an intellectual commitment to a judicial philosophy…or not. What we do know, for certain, is that Originalism typically accrues to the benefit of old, rich, white males, who wrote the constitution and enshrined certain benefits and privileges for themselves. We also know that those who are guided in modern times by an “originalist” framing, for whatever reason, are secure in the notion that our country is best served by rich, old, white males holding disproportionate power and authority. I am a rich, old, white male but I disagree.

comments.name: Gus Bode
comments.body:
Point of (sentence) order. I was confused by this sentence:

“Many district court judges feel like the Supreme Court does not have their backs when they rule against the Trump administration.”

After thinking about it for a while, the “they” are the district court judges. But I read it as the Supreme Court ruling against Trump.

comments.name: Robert Roth
comments.body: I would be very curious to see what   people would do with that example of someone sneaking into a movie theatre. What stories and scenarios and commentaries people would come up with.

comments.name: The Joe smith

comments.name: Blandino
comments.body:
As clear-minded as David French is, he's losing me as a fan with his legal blinders.

Originalism is now, and was before Scalia's cheerleading, a red herring exploited by the right wing to undermine the real and understandable intents of the Constitution:  liberal ideals of late 18th C. political and social thinking.  Does French think a law proposed today that "all men (meaning persons) are created equal" could get through Congress, be signed by the President and survive a Supreme Court challenge?  I don't.  

Another tenet of originalism used to justify laws that keep putting automatic weapons into the hands of schoolchildren is worship of the Second Amendment.  The language is clear to any unbiased reader:  it permits communities to develop armed militias.  It doesn't authorize any rights to concealed carry or the other deranged laws that make public life in America more dangerous than in nearly any other country in the developed world.  Yet every time a state attempts a law limiting access to automatic weapons, Roberts, Alito and their majority stomp on it.  David?  

What should be obvious to any intelligent person, even a lawyer, is that the Constitution was drafted in part responding to inequities, corruption, and religious tyranny of many European countries ruled by royal families.  They chose to imagine an ideal government, and it turned out well.

Watching judicial erosion of the Constitution's ban of an official government religion is even more disturbing.

comments.name: Eric
comments.body:
As expected, the top commenters praise Mamdani’s “courage”- which reflects their skewed view of reality.

Mamdani’s statement on October 7th was a disaster. It didn’t once mention the words “Jew” or “Jewish.” It spent far more time on the aftermath, something Mamdani already does practically every day; he could have easily followed in the footsteps of pretty much all other leaders and kept the focus on the horrors of Oct 7th for ONE day. This is not courage, it is gross insensitivity because of either misguided ideological purity or pressure from his far-left allies. 

And even this was not enough for the protesters, who praised Hamas and chanted death to the IDF. 

It’s entirely possible to acknowledge the atrocities of October 7th without trying to contextualize them, or minimize Jewish pain and suffering. Those who don’t understand this might want to consider that in their desire for moral certainty they have lost their empathy. Once you decide Israelis—and Jews—deserve no empathy, you essentially reinforce Israeli and Jewish fears. 

Of course, Palestinian suffering is real as well and needs to be acknowledged. What happened in Gaza is horrifying as is what is currently happening in the West Bank. These aren’t binaries or zero-sum games; acknowledging complexity and nuance is the more courageous choice, and what we should expect from our leaders.

One used to pay a small premium (say 10% of the ticket price) for the convenience of non-stop, but I recently went to book a flight to Phoenix, more than a month out from the travel date (which was not a holiday of any kind): all the other carriers were charging about $500, and Delta wanted over $1000 *for the basic economy ticket*. comments.name: Declan Moore
comments.body:
The world's decent into a new Cold War has been so slow and gradual as to almost escape notice.  Almost.  There were rumblings: The partial cutoff of oil shipments to Europe in Jan. 2007; Putin's repeated descriptions of the collapse of the USSR as a tragedy.  Then in 2014, Russia seized the Crimea, formerly a part of Ukraine.  The West did nothing.
Today Russia is up to its neck in an attempt to reabsorb Ukraine into the Russian state; an obvious initial step towards the goal of reconstituting the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR), one former Socialist Republic at a time.    Meanwhile China having already militarized the South China Sea, is applying increasing pressure on Taiwan.  They are guaging our response under President Donald Trump.  They like what they see.  
We are in a new Cold War, in a new world, one where China is much stronger than 1950, and U.S. resolve is much weaker.  History has many harsh lessons regarding a nation's failure to respond to external aggression.  In 1938, the unwillingness of Great Britain and France to confront Hitler regarding Germany's seizure of the Sudetenland led directly to the start of World War II.  Today, we have the U.S. under Trump signaling an unwillingness to confront Russia or China regarding their aggressive actions.  All Americans should be both disgusted and terrified by this lack of resolve.  As has been observed many times, those unable to learn from history are condemned to repeat it.

comments.name: Daniel
comments.body: This is a truly exceptional critique of the criticism of Cormac McCarthy.  Its subtlety is a great asset.  One imagines there is good reason for Mr. Woodward’s myth-creating 1992 NYT’s profile and that there is good reason for the selection of facts that make up Tracy Daugherty’s biography.  Neither seem all that accurate but in their inability to nail down the elusive Mr McCarthy, they create an ethereal space that makes McCarthy’s art richer.  Wyatt Mason allows for this, seemingly recognizing its necessity, writing it into his wonderful account of the great novelist.  Doing so, creates another history.

comments.name: Mark Crozier
comments.body:
When I first discovered McCarthy back in the early 90s, the world was a very different place. 

It just so happened Blood Meridian was the first book of his I read (found on a Picador rotunda in a bookstore, the best way to discover a new writer). It was a lightning bolt moment for sure. A blurb on the back cover compared it to Moby Dick. That struck me. It was a Western, after all, a 'genre' not given to much literary critic enthusiasm. It also started me on a lifelong journey to learn more about the author that very much mirrored the way our world has changed. 

Living in South Africa, all I had to go on was the short bio in the books. Who WAS this guy? Attempts to garner information from Picador yielded nothing (they sent me a copy of Child of God, which by then I owned anyway). Some years later when the internet became a thing, I subbed to the New York Times and found the ONE interview. Momentous stuff! By then I'd read everything he'd published. The big reveal came with the Pulitzer for The Road and the subsequent Oprah interview. Staggering at the time, it was.

With today's internet and the likes of YouTube we have access to a vast amount of info. And I will say the mystery is better. The best of an author is almost always found in his books and if it isn't they are doing it wrong. And if you judge them by their relationships you will be sorely disappointed, every time. 

Everything you need to know about McCarthy is in his books. The rest is gossip.

Sometimes you have to go down before you can go up. Dante for example. And for many, our world has become a secular Inferno. When the fire of drones, bombs or deep economic anxiety or hormonal rage, perhaps due to social chaos and injustice, is upon you, upon us, then most, understandably, don't really feel much like reading heavy-duty difficult stuff.

The great Republic of Letters and the growth of a vast readership of literature came about with the increase of not only a leisure class and professional class of writers, but with the belief, and its promotion, that the inner life matters much, and can be elevated to high status not by worldly riches — but by the care of the soul, mind, heart. A mythology for this has died among us. Only its shadow remains. Or the empty snakeskin it left behind.

comments.body:
There hasn’t been anything like the 10-15 yr period after WWll when American literacy improved dramatically, when the GI Bill moved thousands thru college &  vocational schools… when the feds invested heavily in public education, towns & communities flourished. In 1956 the Library Services Act passed providing more funding to both urban & low income areas for library expansion. And between 1960-1970 the Feds provided further significant investment in public & university libraries thru-out the nation.  Coupled with abundant work opportunities for men & with advancements in science improving the nation’s health & longevity ( vaccines ) many families now reaped the benefits that came from steady work, such as building $aving$, acquiring home ownership & finally being able to enjoy a little leisure time. 
Sometimes I thank the stars that my mom & dad aren’t here to witness the decline in both American literacy & civic duty.

comments.name: David L, Jr.
comments.body:
I was intrigued by Richard Weaver's analysis, in The Southern Tradition at Bay, of Southern anti-intellectualism as a thoughtful anti-intellectualism, rather than a simply instinctive one. I find, as someone who is something of an intellectual, that being against the very thing you are - an intellectual - is something akin to the thing I despise the most about Western intellectuals, which is their rush to blame their own society.

I say Bellow's Mr. Sammler's Planet is the most apt book for our time. The target of his ire is the target of mine. He asks "whether the worst enemies of civilization might not prove to be its petted intellectuals who attacked it at its weakest moments -- attacked it in the name of proletarian revolution, in the name of reason, and in the name of irrationality, in the name of visceral depth, in the name of sex, in the name of perfect instantaneous freedom."

Reading divides us and may only speed up our doom and make it more unpleasant. "People become authoritative and plebeians of genius elevate themselves first to nobility and then to universal glory, and all because they had what all poor children got from literacy: ABCs, the dictionary, the grammar books, the classics. Until, soaring from their slums or their little petit-bourgeois parlors, they were addressing worldwide millions. These are the people who set the terms, who make up the discourse, and then history follows their words. Think of the wars and revolutions we have been scribbled into."

comments.name: Leah Barber
comments.body: Congratulations Anne Carson. I’m thrilled that she, who has gifted me so much, in my heart, soul, and mind, is being honored in such a large space. “If Not, Winter” resides perpetually at hand on a corner of my desk. Her choice, to keep alive the spaces between fragments, acknowledges the realities and paradox of life and death; instead of symbolizing the grief of loss, those spaces are embodiments of the infinite. Each lyric, through her poetic translation, is a vessel from the past that holds secrets and vibrant revelation of the here and now. Thank you to a great and inspiring artist.

Also her essays such as on Goya delivered here in Madrid took an original path far from academia to explore a major painting, the sinking dog. Her sintaxis surprises me most of the time. i keep her booklets from Float nearby to browse and breathe. In these dark days it was a joy to hear the news of her Nobel Prize this a.m.

After 65, this can often be a roadblock, and, of course, there are all kinds of remedies and indeed other kinds of intimacy.

comments.name: maybemd
comments.body:
63 when the pandemic started, I was in isolation with a spouse who admitted he couldn't fulfill my current sexual or future age-related physical needs.

My husband wished he could, but just couldn't. He either failed to please or satisfy me, or he'd be stressed out and miserable. Often, both. It had gotten worse over the decades.

A marriage counselor worked with us for two years. He recognized my husband as on the neurodiverse spectrum, taught us what that meant, and found a wonderful therapist for my husband to work with solo.

I realized he is my favorite person in the world. So no, I didn't want to leave him even though I could have readily built a new and satisfying life.

But I didn't want to continue living with him; I needed my own space! And I needed a plan for care in my elder years.

So we began hunting for a senior living community that would provide elder care and a vibrant social life. Life Plan Communities feature independent and assisted living, plus memory and nursing care on a single campus; active resident associations; and all kinds of supportive infrastructure, including salons and massage therapy to provide important physical contact.

We're getting two units: a 2-BR cottage to inhabit, and a studio apartment for my office.

On waiting lists at two communities, we're relieved of burdens we didn't realize we'd been carrying. Especially my husband, who'd been terrified I'd leave him once I recognized his "deficiencies".

It is not unusual for the individual described by the letter writer to not fully understand where he sits on the spectrum.  I had a friend whose husband was diagnosed 10 years into their marriage.  They were committed to each other but struggled until the diagnosis.   This gave both individuals the tools to work together to meet their emotional needs.  

My reaction to the comments is that most commentators want to simplify the cause and effect; gay, cheater, self-absorbed; rather than consider more complex underlying medical reasons that could be addressed with proper diagnosis and therapy.  

This is one perspective that I believe might be surfaced and explored before making the proposed choice offered by the columnist or other commentators.

Divorced at 60 after 29 years of marriage. Met my bf a couple years later. 

We are now both in our late 60s and having a great time, including the best sex of either of our lives. We are both relatively active, creatively generative, enthusiastic about life. 

In reading all these comments, my take away is that there is just no "one way" to age and to partner up.

There are most decidedly other ways to have a close relationship well into one's 80's, which do not require devices or medication.  What was effortless and fun at 30, can be just  be weird at 75.

comments.name: Near the Ocean
comments.body: I think Sharon Horgan is very funny, and the show covers a lot of what is different about being mid-50s versus early 30s, whether it's children or aging parents or a demanding job or a knees that begin to ache. But her character is having a lot of sex, with different people, and she seems to be the object of desire for a lot of different men.  I don't think that's the experience for a lot of women over 50. It's much more a matter of feeling (and being) invisible. It's tough out there.

comments.name: Indisputably
comments.body: I’m happily married. Both my wife and I are athletes in our late 60s, and we have a great sex life (facilitated by hormone replacement therapy). We know many unmarried older people who struggle with dating. I know people of all ages and shapes and sizes and inclinations want or need sexual relationships, but frankly most people our ages just aren’t physically capable of good sex - due to chronic health issues, obesity, lack of fitness, etc. I can imagine this is a real problem when it comes to dating. Of course, if people want to date for simple companionship, that’s a different matter. If they want to remain sexually active, however, it REALLY helps to stay as healthy and fit as possible. I have many old but athletic friends who confirm this. It takes time, effort, and often pain, but at least in my wife’s and my cases we want to stay sexually interested and active as long as we can, so we stay healthy and fit By the way, this applies to younger people as well. I’m appalled by the number of unhealthy, unfit 20- and 30-somethings I see every day. Could this be a reason why so many are not interested in sex?

comments.name: Bruce Bartlett

I learned early on to meet them for coffee rather than regular dinner dates because, despite being very clear about who I am in my profile, we don't click.  They always ask me my politics and seem suspicious on the topic (I was told by one woman that she found that men were hiding their Trump-worship).  I think I expected that they would be bubbly and optimistic, like in high school, but instead are indifferent, weary and wary.  It hasn't been much fun.

comments.name: Tracey Woodruff
comments.body:
Thanks again for speaking with me. I wanted to clarify my quote: there is enough scientific evidence to be concerned about microplastics and to support action to reduce exposures, even as the science continues to develop. Saying the evidence is not yet fully causal does not mean there is no risk. Our rigorous review found that microplastics are suspected to harm human health, and that warrants actions to reduce exposures, whether by individuals or governments, rather than waiting for absolute certainty. Waiting means more exposures to microplastics. 

We also know that many chemicals that are in plastics and can be in synthetic clothing, including PFAS and phthalates, can harm health. And unlike natural fibers, plastics stay persist in the environment and continue to come back to us over time. Talking about synthetic clothing is important, because it is a big part of the fossil fuel to plastic lifecycle so thank you for doing the article.

comments.name: Alice Cook
comments.body:
A lot is missing from this reporting.  It is very difficult to find a causal link between micro exposures of anything to human disease.  We have struggled with this in the water industry.  While we know endocrine disrupting chemicals are in many public water supplies, exposing the population to long term micro doses, it's very difficult to impossible to run a study showing harm.  Same for micro exposures to plastics by wearing say a sports bra. It's very plausible that skin does absorb microplastics from sports bras when it is heated up (plastic is more labile when it's heated).  This is why it's not recommended to put plastic in dishwashers or in dryers.  When heated, it melts and moves around.

This is not MAHA leaning anything- this is just common sense.  If we wait for a causal link between long term exposure of microplastics absorption through skin to human harm, we will be waiting a very long time.  I am not a luxury person or fashion person. But I am someone who thinks about chemistry and what I expose my body to.  I have done my best to reduce phthalates - I don't drink bottled water. And YES I absolutely would love to find a sports bra that is not made of synthetic materials (plastics).  Not luxury, just common sense.  Here's a study on dermal absorption of phthalates from clothes - https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27007912/

And if it takes some early adopters/pioneers spending way more to show us the way in fabric technology, good for them. Let them find the way!

comments.name: MRight
comments.body:
I hate to be so cynical but the fact that influencers are pushing this move to natural fibers makes me think it is just a ploy to sell more clothing. 

Getting rid of perfectly good synthetic clothing and purchasing new natural fibers is wasteful and doesn’t keep anyone safe. Some of that tossed wardrobe is going to end up on the shores of West Africa, where it is going to leach microfibers into the ocean for an eternity. Those fibers are so tiny they evaporate and end up in clouds, then end up raining down on the very person who tossed the clothes in the first place. Purchasing an entire new wardrobe, even if it is thrifted, warms the planet. Heat is more unhealthy than anything. 

There are tradeoffs everywhere in textile manufacturing and garment construction. Cotton is a water hog when it is grown, when it is manufactured into textiles and during garment construction. The dyes pollute local water sources. Synthetic fibers can be spun without so much water.  I have to dry my jeans in the dryer, but all my recycled polyester Athleta separates get line dried. 

The best thing for everyone’s health is to wear the clothing you have until it is no longer usable, and to purchase as little new clothing as possible. Don’t wash your clothes if they aren’t dirty, and line dry. When your  clothes are so worn out you can’t wear them anymore, that is the time to purchase used natural fiber clothing.

As this article points out, pneumonic plague transmission can be frustrated, but doing so would take a toll on everyday living, especially economically and socially. Loners who never near any person or animal and people who wear appropriate masks whenever around anybody or any animal possibly infected would likely be OK. But knowing who or what might be infected and capable of transmitting pneumonic plague would be difficult as any fevered person or animal might could do so if the fever present were due to pestis. Fevers are hard to spot and not always readily noticed even by some people who have one. Seems to me, anyway, that people should always look for the worst possible potential scenario and prepare therefore just to be on the safest side possible… especially when the pathogen involved might be 100% fatal if you are infected thereby.

A simple rule of thumb is to be as precise with one's language as the occasion demands: the highest level of precision is required when lives or money depend on them (and a level of redundancy in the form of an explanation, footnote, or glossary may be desirable).  One can be much less precise in everyday talk, but if one is intentionally careless, it may be difficult to find the right level of precision when the occasion calls for it.  As long as one bears this in mind, all is well... most of the time!  Until then, please pass the schtroumpf!

If it's a pain you will live in pain. Let us also take pleasure in the world, the human condition including sometimes pain, also the artistic and scientific or commonplace conversational work of reducing that. It won't ever be perfect or "right" for good and all. We can make do and have achieved amazingly despite all that remains such a mess. Not happy with people exploiting ambiguity for narrow advantages... In any case, bimonthly is meant to mean every two months but people use it otherwise and usage is a meaning maker too so wherever you go, there you are. It's not that there aren't proper definitions for commonly misused words. It's just that many people are ignorant of them.

Bimonthly means every other month. Semimonthly means twice a month.

Lying prone means lying on one's stomach. Supine is on one's back.

Reticent means hesitant or reluctant to speak. It's not a synonym for reluctant.

Etc., etc. etc. ...

Yes, words eventually mean what the majority come to think they mean. But why essentially eliminate perfectly good words from our lexicon simply because we're too lazy to learn their USEFUL definitions?
