comments.body:
The ultimate claims here seem *wildly* speculative.  The actual findings are that there are a variety of different bacteria in the guts of people who live differently.  But because that isn't an exciting enough claim to get another grant, I guess, the study authors have to start suggesting that maybe those bacteria are responsible for preventing [insert "modern" malady here] possibly sorta we don't actually know.

The microbiome is starting to sound a lot like quantum physics, in that there are about five people who actually understand it, and they aren't the ones making sweeping claims about how it works.

comments.name: Rich Holman
comments.body: One important topic not discussed was the impact on the human mind when the your 35 trillion bacteria are not being fed enough fiber and similar nutrients. As we know, about 90%+ of our serotonin (our happiness drug) is produced in our biome. If those bacteria are not receiving fiber, this production is greatly diminished. Adults in the US now get about 60% of their calories from processed and sugar laden foods and children 70%. The first thing processed food companies do when they receive their corn, soya and wheat is strip out the fiber. Combine this with the fact that excess dopamine (our pleasure drug) in our systems constrict the dopamine receptors in our brains. Thus we are producing less serotonin and it is being restricted by our excess dopamine.  Sugar by the way acts similar to stimulating our dopamine receptors like cocaine. Now look at the increasing numbers of mental issues in the US (depression, dementia, Alzheimers, ADHD, autism, bi polar, etc.) where about 25% of women are taking SSRI´s.  This is an area or research that should not be ignored.,

comments.name: SEH
comments.body: Wasn't the average lifespan of our ancestors like, 30?

comments.name: Jen
comments.body: Have an autoimmune disease? Read Epidemic of Absence. Understand the gut is the center of our immune systems. Think about how different ecosystems are when you remove the megafauna. Worms were the elephants in our gut’s  “savannah.” Not only did they affect the other species present, they affected the geography itself through chemical signals. Those same signals helped us make t regulatory cells. T regs are the part of your immune system that calms inflammation. T regs stop the police brutality that is autoimmunity. When you take Cipro, you shift your microbiome from a jumpy one to a hostile one, and you never get back some of the friendlies. When they are gone, you might not be able to make enough butyrate or Urolithin a in your colon. Ever again. Thus more autoimmune problems. The doc who prescribed you Cipro thinks the infection itself triggered the autoimmune disease you have for the rest of your life. Nope. Killing all the gentle organisms who act like compost does in the soil of your guts did. Can you go out and get worms and fix it? Not for most people, unfortunately. We do need to study the chemical signals the worms gave us though. And we should be collecting these diverse microbe samples and making targeted probiotics to restore our immune systems. Problem is no patent. No money. Just health.

comments.name: beh
comments.body: Is it possible that our changing digestive environment is actually helping us survive our polluted world?

comments.name: nastyboy
comments.body:
"Its composition shifted hundreds of thousands of years ago when early humans started cooking with fires, scientists suspect."

Equals HCAs and PAHs. Seems this has been bad for many people. Fortunately chemistry has stepped up with medication for everything.

comments.name: Saffron
comments.body: This article contributes to the notion that we live in a world of decline from a perfect past moment. I doubt the scientists involved would agree. The comments below illustrate how this feeds an unhealthy bias towards cataclysmic thinking.

comments.name: Fe
comments.body: My sister calls it the Standard American Diet, S.A.D., this is why I grow my own vegetables and the majority of the food I eat I make, I am still 30lbs heavier than I need to be but at 60 am in much better shape than the majority of those in my age range and I am not on any pills for blood pressure, diabetes whatever, in fact I am on no medication at all.

articles.title: Was the Human Gut Healthier in Ancient Times?
articles.summary: The microbiome isn’t what it used to be in many parts of the world. The shift may be affecting the well-being of people in industrialized countries.

comments.name: Katie Fisk
comments.body: Procrastinator is definitely a word I would use to describe myself but it's not a word others describe me as. What I mean by this is I am unfortunately pretty good at procrastination to the point that unless I tell someone that I put it off until the night before it's due they wouldn't know. Often the reason I find myself procrastinating is that I feel frozen almost in a petrified state that what if I start something and figure out I don't know how? or maybe that I can't do it well enough? or what if my best attempts turn out to just disappoint others? There are nights where I am up until 2am stressing trying to finish homework I have pushed off until the very very last minute yet somehow I manage to always pull it off and mask the exhaustion too. Procrastination is definitely something I struggle with and something lots of people struggle with because unfortunately the best motivation is often a too close deadline and the only solution to maintain the perfect appearance of being pulled together is a super late night grind.

comments.name: Anjaly Romero
comments.body: Yes, procrastination is my baddest habit. I procrastinate everything, like my homework, house chores, being on time for certain events, etc. Why do I do it? It might be a combination of a lot of things. Maybe very poor time management, laziness, and fear. I think about doing it more than actually doing it which has led to negative outcomes. When it comes to school work, putting off my assignments and homework makes my performance in school bad. I usually get assignments given to me way before the actual due date and yet I do it the day before leaving me stressed out and not enough time to do my assignment with the best work I could've given. I do hope to leave this bad habit before I go into college, I do not want to take this habit with me.

comments.name: Madeline
comments.body: I am a huge procrastinator or in other words I love to exaggerate the time I have. In one way I give myself too much time. I’m very type A so I always like to be early but I always over exaggerated how much time it actually takes. In the same way I can be the opposite though. Something could be due at 12 and I said I was gonna do it at 3 but then I put it off because I think I have time. When I actually get to it then I realize that I need way more time. Also if something happens I like to make it more than it is. There’s no reason for it, I just end up doing it

comments.name: Giselle Figueroa
comments.body: I am very much a procrastinator, it is my greatest fault and weakness. It is a huge thing that crosses into my daily life as much as it consumes my academic life. It causes me to forget getting a birthday present for my friend, signing up for an activity I was looking forward to and even putting off self-care that I need by the end of the week. The article says that finding one thing and sticking to it routinely, let it cycle settle and watch that good habit reach into other things- however it’s important to note that for procrastinators; it’s difficult to stick to even one routine. I’ve noticed that with people who avoid doing tasks, the hardest part is starting a task- not necessarily doing it to completion. Forcing these habits and cycles, the effort to keep up with them is the most difficult part of someone who gets easily distracted and discouraged.

comments.name: Lucia Popp
comments.body: No, procrastinating is a bad habit that students, especially teenagers, need to break. Procrastinating saves all the work for the last minute, then it is poorly done and the worker is more stressed than they would be if the work was done when it was assigned. There are reasons upon reasons why being a procrastinator is deficient, and yet I am very much a procrastinator myself. I love to wait until the last minute to complete an assignment although I know it will just stress me out more. I was assigned a presentation 2 months ago due this Wednesday and decided to start it Sunday night. I stay busy, I am incredibly busy, but holding off to do my work is my worst habit. Procrastinating is not something easy to rid yourself of. I wish I could go into study hall, do all of my work, and go home with nothing else to do, but I do not. Instead, 10pm on a Thursday night after 5 hours of dance seems like the better option. This is something I will break myself of, hopefully before college.

comments.name: Jack
comments.body: In this day and age procrastination takes over the lives of countless people including me and a lot of students which is partly thanks to the rise of technology. When a student gets home from a long day of school the easiest thing to do is go lay down and scroll for hours on social media instead of starting the homework they were supposed to do. This problem has taken many hours of productive time in the afternoon from me as the assignments I should be doing linger in the back of my mind. Yet many people argue that it is a problem of laziness which is definitely partly true. However I believe the addictive nature of phones and social media is more to blame, along with the exhausting nature of school.

comments.name: Noah
comments.body: I feel like procrastination can be a very helpful tool to use, although it may sometimes seem lazy. Many people view procrastination as putting things off, as a way of postponing any work that must be done. But I feel like even though that is a definition of procrastination, it does not detail the whole story. I think that procrastination can help when it comes to activities. Not everyone gets the activity at the first try and little bit of procrastination can help you unconsciously problem solve within your mind, helping you brainstorm ideas and foster creativity, allowing you to come back to the same activity with even more determination. Circling back to it, I agree that procrastination can be negative when it comes to certain activities, such as some that have some sort of priority within them. But the positive outcome of taking some time to rethink the same problems from a different perspective with more energy, can help you work twice as hard.

comments.name: Mohammad
comments.body: I admit, I am a procrastinator, but I don’t see it as a bad thing. At least, when it’s in moderation. I procrastinate on mainly homework, sometimes household chores, but I still manage to get them done at a reasonable time. I can look at an assignment, feel the sense of dread overcome me, and decide not to do it, but when it matters, I feel energized enough to get it done. See, procrastination can be both good because of how restful it can be, and bad because of the lack of productivity. When I procrastinate usually depends on the urgency of the situation. I have the ability of assertiveness over myself after a level or urgency, so that when I know this is when I need to get it done, I’ll get it done, and sometimes I’ll use incentives. However, rarely will you see me take the “proactive approach” and just get it done as soon as I can so I can rest later. If I have free time in my schedule to fit in, it’s going to be here and now. However, I am considering the ideas in the newsletter. You can think of it as a chain reaction. When one thing happens, the next one also happens, and so on. So, if you get one step done, you might just end up doing the next step.

articles.title: Are You a Procrastinator?
articles.summary: Do you find it hard to get started on tasks? Does the urge to postpone and delay make things harder for you?

comments.name: Human
comments.body: Adam Nagourney, thanks for including this: “in much of the classical music world, Mr. Botstein is better regarded as a curator than as a conductor.” That’s putting it mildly. Musicians with whom he has worked view him as an incompetent dilettante. The fact that he was able to build a concert hall at Bard and rule over it as his fiefdom for decades says a lot about the classical music world. Money talks.

comments.name: Joe Pearce
comments.body: To be honest about it, I never even heard of Bard before Leon Botstein became associated with it, and have really never read anything about Bard since that wasn't associated with Leon Botstein. Is it a great seat of learning on its own, or is it just a great seat of learning because it has been associated with Leon Botstein for a half-century?

comments.name: Times Reader 1978
comments.body: The fact that Leon Botstein still has a job in any public venue is a disgrace. He should NOT be leading the American Symphony Orchestra or have any other musical position. He is a disgrace, and the fact that Bard allowed him to remain as long as they did even after resigning as president is also a disgrace. I hope his other "employers" will see the light. He needs to go away.

comments.name: B
comments.body:
The letter subsequently sent by ongressman Raskin to Bard's current acting President sheds further light on this concern:
https://democrats-judiciary.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/democrats-judiciary.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/2026-10-07-raskin-to-weber-becker-bard-re-botstein.pdf

comments.name: David G
comments.body:
Sad, sad, sad. I’ve been attending the Bard music festivals and programs for decades, since I live in the Hudson Valley.

Botstein has been indispensable to the institution. For many years — no Botstein, no Bard.

Of course, he shouldn’t have been buddying around with Epstein, despite the probability of losing a major source of revenue. He didn’t display good judgment with that decision.

But Botstein, who did nothing illegal, has now been canceled.

Cancel Culture is just as insidious as openly carousing with a felon. These are the times we live in.

I won’t be attending Bard anymore. Let Botstein’s replacement dredge up the funds.

comments.name: Henry
comments.body: College and university presidents typically have retreat rights, that is the right to a tenured professorship with all that entails, including appropriate sabbaticals to work on projects, which do benefit the institution (pace one commentator below).  Unless Prof. Botstein has violated conditions of his employment, he may not be disciplined, let alone fired.  Many people outside academia hate tenure, mainly because they do not understand it, but it has been crucial pillar of the success story of American higher education, the best system in the world, i.e. until the debacles of the last two years.

comments.name: Al from PA
comments.body: Botstein was really great at "selling the sizzle." He was a musicologist whose conducting attracted a lot of attention to the college--it was the "equivalent of a football team." But selling sizzle means selling the great smell of cultural capital shared between donors, educators, students, and the public. When the sizzle turns to stench it's all over.

comments.name: J R
comments.body: I think Mr. Edelman himself should kiss Botstein’s feet! Good lord!

articles.title: Forced to Retire Over Epstein, Ex-College Leader Keeps Campus Ties
articles.summary: Leon Botstein is no longer president of Bard College, but he continues to teach and play a prominent role in the school’s signature music programs.

comments.name: Vincent Zhang
comments.body: Flock Cameras have always been a thought of mine. I had heard of the concept from social media, and I am mixed about them. However, what stands out to me is that it records your every move, and I wonder about the ethics. The concept is great. Having “mini-robot police officers” watching crime and alerting officials could potentially make the world a much more peaceful place. However, it depends on the client. Some can detect crimes, while others strip away the privacy of everyday life, so you never know what a Flock camera is doing. So, when they spread across the U.S., it’s concerning, to say the least. Flock’s supporters say it’s helpful for the police, while some say it’s unregulated mass surveillance.  Both are very persuasive, as they could perfectly be used for both purposes. And as the opposition grows, it’s understandable. If you don’t know what a Flock camera is using, most people assume the worst. However, with vandalism, I don’t support it, because it’s someone else’s property and a blatant felony, but it shows the public’s concern over a watching camera. If a Flock camera popped out in my neighborhood, I would not want it to be present, because I usually get concerned when something spies on me. It’s an endless cycle of “Helpful” and “Stripping away privacy”, and what really should be done is to stop violence before it starts, like to not promote violence as “cool”

comments.name: Maddy
comments.body: I think that people vandalizing these Flock cameras is crazy. It is not to watch you specifically, it is to help keep the public safe. I mean if someone has a camera at their house and it faces their driveway and the street, and you walk past are you going to start freaking out because its “Invading your privacy” like people say flock cameras do in the article? I don't think for a moment that any of these oppositions are justified. The cameras are not physically hurting anyone. Sure it is okay to question why any person in the public has access to the flock camera's information, however it should never lead to destroying things that you didn't pay for.

comments.name: Benton
comments.body: I think it's creepy having Flock cameras in the U.S. just because of how they are being used. Yes, it's fine if it's to find the bad people on the roads who drive really crazy. As they said in the article, " a brand of automated license plate readers that employ artificial intelligence to identify and track vehicles has divided the public and rattled civil liberties watchdogs.” This means your license plate can just be found by a camera on the road that is gonna randomly show up and get you a ticket through the mail. This is an invasion of privacy i think.

comments.name: Sam
comments.body: The rise of surveillance technology and the use of flock cameras is one of the biggest threats to American freedom. Flock cameras can limit crime but as Engle says “ …the information can be dangerous in the wrong hands.” One important thing with Flock and crime is that sometimes the AI is wrong and can falsely accuse someone for a crime they didn’t even commit, like the cases where people get accused of stealing cars when they really didn’t. The whole thing with Flock is reminiscent of a quote by Benjamin Franklin where he said "Those who would give up essential Liberty, to purchase a little temporary Safety, deserve neither Liberty nor Safety."

comments.name: Lily
comments.body: This is the first time I heard about flock cameras. I feel like it's a hard argument on whether they should be set up or not. I personally don’t think i would want one in my neighborhood, because i think it would creep me out and make me feel like i was being stalked, hearing stories like tracking ex girlfriends/boyfriends, and trying to arrest people for getting abortions traveling to different states which is insane! Although there’s many risks i do also think it would be very useful if used by the right people to capture criminals just like in the groups magazine using “crime-fighting star” when talking about the flock cameras.

comments.name: ES
comments.body: The arguments for the plate readers are not very persuasive in my opinion. “License plate readers”? Since when have devices designed to “read license plates” needed to look at nearby companies' databases in order to find users with customer rewards in order to correlate passing vehicles and track down individuals? And sure, maybe that could be used to track down criminals, but it hasn't. Recently, there have been multiple murders in Minneapolis — a city filled with Flock cameras — and yet, no Flock cameras have come to the rescue. Their real purpose is to create mass surveillance, not for civilian protection.

comments.name: Leah
comments.body: I personally do not believe in the use of flock cameras. In “Flock Cameras Are Dividing U.S. Cities. Here’s What to Know About Them.,” It’s stated that they use artificial intelligence to use them. I think that is a really bad idea because AI is not always right. I remember hearing about a woman who was swatted by police because a flock camera had flagged her car down as stolen, but it was the wrong person. I also don’t believe that they only use them for license plates. It scares me with how easy they could be hacked into which would give out all our information.

comments.name: Courtney
comments.body: I have heard about the debate of Flock Cameras, but I didn’t know exactly what they were until now. Based on this new information, I believe that Flock Cameras could have benefits but also a lot of negatives. I think it is an important goal to try to prevent and track down criminals, but many people do not want to be under constant surveillance. In the article, “Flock Cameras Are Dividing U.S. Cities. Here’s What to Know About Them.”, Neil Vigdor states, “They produce a trove of highly sophisticated surveillance records instantly. While proponents say this helps prevent crime, opponents say the information can be dangerous in the wrong hands.”. I would not want cameras to be set up in my neighborhood. I don’t want footage to be spread or shared without consent. As citizens of the United States I believe that we deserve privacy. These Flock Cameras, as mentioned in the article, are testing the 4th Amendment. These cameras for preventing crime should cause people to be unnecessarily searched or wrongfully convicted.

articles.title: How Concerned Are You About the Growing Use of Surveillance Technology?
articles.summary: Flock Safety cameras, used by thousands of law enforcement agencies in the U.S., have drawn intense criticism from civil liberties groups. Do they help reduce crime or threaten our privacy?

comments.name: suevv
comments.body: Mirror Mirror episode of original Star Trek (1967)? Pondering what it foretold and - more interesting to the topic at hand - why the mirror images were so different. Brilliant sci fi from before chiral molecules were really understood the way they are today.

comments.name: Mixilplix
comments.body: God bless scientists.

comments.name: MikeMikeMike
comments.body: We could potentially apply this to food chemistry and prevent all sorts of illnesses and ailments. Just some food for thought.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body:
Congratulations to both researchers on one of the most important subjects in organic chemistry. Talk of chirality , enantiomers, etc.. takes me back to the late 80's when I was taking an O-Chem class in college - it was interesting when we learned -L-amino acids -"Left-handed" -were the only form found in nature. I was fortunate I had a teacher who looked at the consequences of nature , not just emphasizing dry organic synthesis pathways, which badly taught O-Chem classes can become.

Another added bonus of the Soai Reaction is it conclusively lays waste to the "Intelligent Design" Theory favored by creationists and anti-science Christians who believe God designed nature , so the fact all amino acids are left-handed is proof to them of a designer. Dr. Soai showed that breaking symmetry - chirality - by unguided, random processes can lead to replicable imbalances in nature ,e.g.,- L-Amino Acids.

Overall a great day for science. Too bad most Americans couldn't care less.

articles.title: Nobel Prize Is Awarded for Pioneering Work in ‘Mirror’ Chemistry
articles.summary: The Nobel Committee recognized Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for solving a century-old mystery about molecules with mirror images. Their work is crucial for pharmaceuticals and carries clues to the origins of life.

comments.name: Bayricker
comments.body: “As Europe combats climate change” Really? They can combat it all they want but will lose because humans cannot control the climate any more than controlling the cycles of the Sun, Moon and the Stars.

comments.name: Prester John
comments.body: The Europeans could have sided with Trump and had the combined weight of the US and Europe to counter China.

comments.name: individual 1
comments.body: The Chinese government aims to maximize exports to Europe while minimizing imports from the continent, seeking to maintain a favorable trade balance. It is advisable for no nation to permit an unbalanced influx of Chinese goods without corresponding reciprocal imports. Engaging with China in trade requires caution, as there is a risk of economic exploitation, potential social and political leverage, and, in certain circumstances, strategic or military implications.

comments.name: Randall Pouwels
comments.body: How has China come to control the corner of rare earths so completely? Are those minerals found only in mainland China?

comments.name: VacuumLight
comments.body: My college pals in Germany prefer to work 6 hours per day, and in service sector. All of them. That culture won't survive long.

comments.name: Deepak
comments.body: Mao pulled China out of poverty in his Great Leap Forward pulling it ahead of much of the developing world by many basic metrics like health,hunger and education. This is the first important thing to note. From this foundation has arisen an Industrial colossus that the West now has to reckon with. The only drawback to this being China's one child policy from the Cultural Revolution which has lead to a coming Demographic decline.

comments.name: Fred
comments.body: No country on the planet can compete with a country that exports products, such as autos, for less money than it costs to produce them. The only way to stop that is to forbid the products from entering your country. But then you wind up groveling for necessary things such as heavy metals. All because we thought it a good idea to send all our production to China for a savings of $20.00 on a TV or 50cents on a t-shirt. And that country was nobody's friend at the time. Who gives an adversary their business in a local deal?

comments.name: SRMT
comments.body: There are indications of possible dumping of Chinese products.  It wouldn't be surprising;  the regime faces a financial crisis that the rest of the world doesn't seem very aware of, and has responded largely by pushing exports at all costs, as this article says, and by continuing the old strategy of building lots of infrastructure whether it's needed or not.

articles.title: Europe’s Trade Tensions With China Are Coming to a Head
articles.summary: The European Union is weighing tougher trade measures as negotiators prepare to meet Chinese officials in Beijing, with surging exports from China pressuring key industries in Europe.

comments.name: keb
comments.body: Four years!?  four years out of college. I was still waiting tables. But I retired with a (low) six figure salary, and a retirement plan that offers me a very comfortable middle class life. of course, my first apartment was $90 a month… I know things are different now

comments.name: David
comments.body: Rich kids have the most opportunities leading to college admissions. They go to exclusive universities, mostly composed of other wealthy folks. Not doubting their talent but rich kids become rich adults.

comments.name: Jean K
comments.body: I'm a little confused about how they classified what people earned after their major. For example, what about people with English majors who went to law or medical school...they clearly make much higher salaries on average than what was listed in this database? What jobs did they consider for inclusion after a given major; only those that directly pertained to that major?

comments.name: Walter
comments.body:
Obviously, your degree or the institution that conferred it matters far less than what you do with the knowledge and relationships you gained in school.

Median-income statistics are not useful to me. My peers with Philosophy degrees include lawyers earning well over $1 million a year, teachers who earn far less, and people in business, from CEOs and salespeople to wonderfully happy Costco warehouse workers.

As Americans, we do not like to admit it, but the circumstances of our birth, the fortune we encounter along the way, the character of our spouses, and even our physical appearance matter a great deal, too. So my advice is to have fun in college, build friendships and marry well, and do what feels fun and easy (what you enjoy and are exceptionally good at).

comments.name: Allison
comments.body:
"I would rather universities and departments be judged not simply by how well their graduates do for themselves, but by how much value they create for others: how much they contribute to society, who benefits from that labor and whether that work is improving people’s lives."

If only the value created for others translated into value created for yourself. Then teachers would be highly paid and wall street bankers would be working class. In fact, the share of output that goes to labor has steadily decreased over the past several decades and we've all decided we're okay with that. And so universities and departments will continue to be judged the way everything else in this country is judged - the bottom line.

comments.name: C
comments.body:
This data is ancient history. AI is killing most of the jobs, except maybe AI related ones.  

Learn how to think critically and find your passion in college. That will probably serve you much better than a somewhat larger salary that might not materialize anyway.

comments.name: Anna
comments.body: “I would rather universities and departments be judged not simply by how well their graduates do for themselves, but by how much value they create for others: how much they contribute to society, who benefits from that labor and whether that work is improving people’s lives.”  Those are beautiful ideas by Dr. Herschlag. Yes that would be ideal.

comments.name: Noah Ravens
comments.body: The 17 graduate detail is the most useful line in this piece. Medians from small cohorts swing hard, so families should look at the spread for a major, not the top school. Using the same Scorecard data, the middle 80% of math programs land between about $56,000 and $97,000. Civil engineering programs sit in a tight $78,000 to $94,000 band almost regardless of school. Nursing is the opposite: the nine highest earning programs are all in California, so the state matters more than the name. I build a free planning tool called Light My Career that plots every program in a major so students can see where a school actually lands. The pattern is clear: for some majors the school matters enormously, and for others it barely matters.

articles.title: At Nearly $300,000, Some Recent Duke Graduates Out-Earned All Their Peers
articles.summary: Federal data show Duke math majors earning a bigger median income four years after graduation than any other majors from any school. It’s a small cohort.

comments.name: Alpen Tree
comments.body: Even poor people clean their houses and wash their clothes.

comments.name: Bob
comments.body: Is this gonna be streaming, & on what streaming channel, or in theaters or what?

comments.name: Robin
comments.body: Considering how infrequently people bathed in the 18th century the main thing that cannot be portrayed on any screen is what they smelled like.

comments.name: mathman'sdaughter
comments.body: I loved the  Ang Lee version and I'm looking forward to this one.

comments.name: Liesl
comments.body: It was such a revelation to download a collection of Jane Austen; in reading S & S and P & P, I found that I could easily follow the conversation, sentence structure and story flow. The past 30 years has produced modern film scripts that often closely follow the original dialogues. How could a young woman (21 years old in the late 1790s), write with such skill that it translates beautifully to our 2026 emotions and understanding? Although she apparently worked on her manuscripts for another decade before being published, she is a remarkable author for the ages. Now I'm hoping to see a P and P set in an African storyline. Hoping for some "beyond white" versions.

comments.name: Rena
comments.body: Personally, I don't like all these dark stagings. Yes, it may be period accurate, but being of a certain age, ambient darkness makes everything much harder to see and experience. This goes for live performances, too...

comments.name: cmk
comments.body:
Reminds me of the "different approach" of the 2005 film of Pride and Prejudice (Knightley and McFayden): messy hair, messy clothes, a lack of eighteenth century basic manners by everyone regardless of occasion.  The romance was all so breathless.  It was as if they were all Bronte-ized. 

Seems as if directors of the newer versions of Austen fear the actual period and its decorum, which is ironic because her humor depends on it.

comments.name: Chris R
comments.body: The BBC is known for not glamning up the actors in anything, including contemporary police procedurals. Unlike say, Rookie FBI where the main character dressed in skintight cleavage revealing clothing and wore heavy makeup. It's one of the many things I like about the Beeb

articles.title: Crafting a Grittier, Grimier ‘Sense and Sensibility’
articles.summary: A new adaptation dispenses with period glamour in favor of a lived-in feel and realism. The goal is to bring emotions to the fore.

articles.title: Margaret Hamilton, Who Developed Software for First Moon Landing, Dies at 90
articles.summary: Her work enabled NASA’s Apollo onboard computers to alert astronauts of problems.

comments.name: Jennifer Morton
comments.body: What a remarkable woman!

comments.name: Joe Tylicki
comments.body:
In an era when computers and people rarely interacted directly...

Indeed.  At 60, I'm old enough to be taught to program using punch cards.  The HMI was a machine the size of an attorney's desk that you fed the cards in to, ran your program, and then printed off the results.

What's with Wizard of Oz comments?  She is very attractive to go with her smarts.  I don't think Bruce would stand a chance.

comments.name: TheIcemanCometh
comments.body:
I transferred from a small college to a major state university to complete my degree (their names are not material). At that university several friends lived in fraternities. In fact one of the house mothers was one of my high school teacher's real mother. 

Even with that I eschewed joining and living in a fraternity. Instead I decided to live a co-op. The co-op houses were owned by the university but managed by the students. They also had a live in resident.

The best way to describe that co-op system is that it was no different than the greek system. There were social events with drinking, there was hazing, etc. The only difference is that there were no greek names and perhaps not quite as much peer pressure to participate. I made it clear that I would not participate in any of the hazing. I rarely participated in the social events as I was dating someone.

I lived there a year then got my own apartment. I would have moved out sooner but could not afford it or the penalties of breaking the contract.

The university later disbanded the co-op system because it was not self sustaining cost wise.  I had mixed feelings. One hand it gave some middle ground between dormitories, fraternities, and fully independent living. But it also had some downsides.

As for the Cornell case, it was handled poorly, very poorly. Administrative heads need to removed.

They kept a very low profile and I would be surprised if most of the students even gave much thought to them.

“Members have to be selected to join, making them seem prestigious and giving existing members more power.“

I was a lifeguard at my college's pool when I was in school, and every year before the Greek Games swim meet we had to remind fraternity and sorority members of the pool rules, specifically the ban on diving into the shallow end of the pool.  I would hear without fail every year, "Well, I'm in Such-And-Such fraternity/sorority and I have to practice for the swim meet", as if their membership conferred some sort of special privilege to ignore the rules.  Telling them that it would be hard for them to participate in the meet if they were banned from the pool generally did the trick.

comments.name: Dr Arun Prasad
comments.body:
1. Over-reliance on AI may reduce the surgeon’s own vigilance, judgement and operative skills.
2. AI errors or false reassurance could lead to incorrect dissection and catastrophic injury.
3. Unusual anatomy and complex cases may fall outside the AI’s training data, making its recommendations unreliable.
4. Liability becomes unclear—if an AI recommendation contributes to harm, responsibility may be difficult to determine.
5. Patient safety and ethics remain concerns regarding data privacy, informed consent, algorithmic bias and inadequate human oversight.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
When I was a student, my best professors and teachers were older people with real-life industry experience.  They had seen firsthand many different situations not covered in the textbook and knew how to deal with them.  What worked and didn't work.  They taught us well.

I think surgeons (and doctors in general) would be best taught by competent experienced professionals.  Using A.I. makes me nervous.  Where did the A.I. obtain its "training"?  What is its source materials?  How is that source information edited?

Note that the human body is far from uniform.  Different people react differently to medications and surgical procedures.  Some people are lucky and heal quickly, others heal slowly with complications that need special attention.  One size does not fit all.

Given my own modern experiences with computers, including A.I. in a medical environment, I am very nervous about it.  For instance, A.I. asks me questions, but does not understand my responses.  It can only check off boxes, not interpret nuances the way a trained human can.

Heck, the computer can't even process the bills correctly.  That's basic computer science.  So, if they can't get that working, how can we expect the computer industry to get A.I. right, which is far more complex?

comments.name: hen3ry
comments.body: I think that this is an excellent way to use A.I. in medical settings.  I wouldn't want doctors to become too dependent on A.I. and lose the ability to make diagnoses, do surgery, or think on their feet.  But for something like this, where it helps surgeons avoid making mistakes, A.I. is appropriate.  I hope our wealthcare system appreciates that and doesn't force us to go through A.I. before we see a doctor.

comments.name: CitizenJ
comments.body:
Not my field, but this seems a sensible use of a well-trained AI model. It can iterate tirelessly to get better at this task. A computer trained on a digital image can already detect things better than the human eye. With training, and guardrails, and overseen by a human, it will make such judgements faster than a human. The human can double check the result before making a final decision.  
    In the same vein, AI can help identify microfractures in bones. I had a tiny break in my wrist. No human noticed the break. A week later, when I was still in pain, the human revisited my x-ray and found a microfracture. A well trained AI model could have looked longer than t the human, the first time, found the fracture, and helped me start healing sooner. This will still need a human to supervise the AI examination, it seems.  
    I would defer to the medical experts. They will know which approach works best, and be motivated to use the approach that is best for the patient. NOT what makes the most profit for an AI company.

comments.body: This woman may have been convicted of a crime decades ago, but in America, she still has her Constitutional rights.  The exact extent of those rights it would seem is still, after 250 years, somewhat unclear.  But it IS clear that no one for any reason should be tortured when being executed.  That the full extent of the torturous treatment that this woman IN FACT received may not have been intended does not change the fact of its effects upon her and she is and at all times was a human.  She has paid her price and much more.  That she suffered and struggled to breathe for at least an hour, and probably for 90 minutes, while staff stood around waiting for her to die before calling an ambulance is an atrocity that casts shame on all of us.

comments.name: Mmm
comments.body:
I don't think the death penalty is immoral or unconstitutional.  It's been practiced for thousands of years.  It is used by the military.  It is expressly countenanced by the Bible and the Koran.   I think it probably best serves a functional purpose as leverage to get murders to plead down to life imprisonment and avoid the expense of a capital murder trial.

I also think the state should devise a better means to carry out executions.   I would even be sympathetic to commuting Ms. Pike's sentence at this point, not because this episode absolves her guilt for the murder she committed, but as redress for the state's incompetence.  

The condemned should be entitled to a solemn execution carried out in a professional manner that respects the human dignity of the dying, whatever evil may lie in their hearts.

comments.name: Ben
comments.body:
These articles tend to bury the lede a bit about how she tortured and killed someone, had absolutely zero remorse at the time and arguably still feels no remorse whatsoever, and tried to kill another inmate while she was at it. She no doubt had a horrendous childhood herself, as many people do who do not later torture and kill their classmates and then show up to the crime scene laughing and asking the police if there are any suspects while bragging to their classmates. Calling for her release is absolutely baffling. 

The real story is the sheer incompetence of correctional facilities. Some prisoners certainly deserve to die, but our system is not capable of doing it and to sentence anyone to death by such grossly incompetent people is a clear violation of the 8th amendment. Commute her sentence to life without parole and let's move on already.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body:
The insanity of this is really something else.  No matter how you feel about the death penalty, we have very effective ways of ending another person's life.   If you want to use drugs, we have (sadly) endless evidence of drugs that are very quickly lethal and cause so little pain (in fact, unbelievable pleasure and euphoria) that people "test" them on a daily basis to deadly effect.   There are 100's (perhaps 1000's) of opiates out there that produce a quick and relatively peaceful death, don't require IV injection (if fact, some are so potent that they don't require an injection at all) and are widely used in medicine.   

This isn't some "mystery" and it's not that hard, in fact it's so easy that people accidentally do it regularly!    We also have plenty of OD reports from survivors who basically all tell the same story, "I just went to sleep", no pain, no burning in arm, no awful complications (well, other than death, but, in this case, that's the point).

It's absolutely ridiculous and frankly unacceptable that we're not using drugs that we KNOW work quickly, effectively and painlessly for this purpose.   Honestly, you could probably just  give death row inmates as much of a pure opiate supply as they'd like and just wait for nature to take it's course.

comments.name: Braden
comments.body: Seems to me that prospective home buyers have already gone over the psychological cliff, particularly younger first time homebuyers who are now confronted with a growing list of hurdles including rising home prices, stagnating wages, steeply rising mortgage interest rates, rising insurance rates, as well as inflating prices for everything else such as fuel, food, healthcare, and major purchases such as automobiles. It's enough to make them despair of ever owning a home. Rising interests rates pose a particularly stark psychological barrier because they are immediately reflected in monthly payments. Given the general sense of increasing economic anxiety,  it's easy to see how potential buyers are getting spooked. There does not appear to be any relief on the interest rate horizon, and if anything things look like they could get worse. A good case can be made for the huge surge in AI related spending is a major contributor to increases interest rates and that does not show any signs of abating soon. A historically large and increasing federal debt does not help either and we can thank Trump and the Republicans for that as well via the recently passed tax bill which was predicted to increase deficits as it certainly has. So here we are, rising interest rates and inflation everywhere else you turn. It's a painful scenario without any realistic pathway towards relief in sight.

To add to that we both had secure jobs, I a hospital RN, my husband, a good position as a marine biologist for the CA Dept. of Fish and Wildlife.  It is no longer the same, by any measure.  That small home of ours is now worth a million dollars.   Plus jobs are no longer secure.  These young adults not only here in CA but across the nation are faced with jobs that could be taken from them in a nano-second, rising housing costs, as well as interest rates.  We are doing an injustice to millions of Americans when we compare our past affordability, which it was, to this present paradigm.  Oh, and our federal government was not as corrupted back then as it is now.  We never faced this unconscionable burgeoning oligarchic autocracy.

comments.name: George
comments.body:
From our condo unit we see the Chrysler Building amongst the East Midtown skyline and I always wonder about its fate.

The beauty of the exterior does mask the fact that as a nearly 100-year old office structure its columned floor plans speak of a very different era than the open office ideal of today.

This drawback is akin to the rival Empire State Building, which, built at the same time, just topped the Chrysler as the then tallest building -- even as Chrysler's last minute spire pushed up late one night sought to prove otherwise.

The building's small floor plans likely makes it a difficult "sell" in attracting tenants albeit the cachet of the building remains undeniable.

Tishman Speyer will face a challenging task despite a full renovation and the provision of a terraced lounge by the 61st Story's eagle gargoyles.  But those who cherish it's Art Deco style truly hope they succeed.

That Art Deco look is, IMO, now complemented by the very modernistic One Vanderbilt tower just a couple of blocks away.  Together they serve to show that East 42nd Street, home too of Grand Central Terminal, remains a vital commercial thoroughfare in this most fascinating city.

Kudos also to Cooper Union for finding a true hometown tenant to take on the ground lease.  150 year term is a bit unusual but with likely rent escalator clauses will provide a welcome endowment to preserve its tuition free status.

India’s young population could be its greatest economic asset, but only if the country can turn young people into productive, employable workers. Otherwise, the same demographic advantage could become a liability.

 The concern is particularly important now because AI is arriving at exactly the time when India has a very large number of young people entering the workforce. India has an enormous base of engineers, IT workers, English speakers, and digitally connected young people.

The World Bank reports that India’s youth account for roughly 72% of the unemployed, and that there is a substantial mismatch between what young people are trained to do and what employers need.

  There is also a deeper structural problem: India has not created enough productive manufacturing and formal-sector jobs to absorb its enormous labor force.

  The future looks bleak for many highly educated young Indians unless they can find opportunities abroad in countries such as the USA, Canada, Europe, and other developed nations. However, immigration policies in these countries are becoming increasingly selective.

  I do not expect the Indian government to come up with an easy solution to this problem. Student protests are likely to continue, irrespective of which government is in power.

One, for example, is when my youngest daughter - who is afraid of heights - flew through the air on a trapeze. At that moment I was inspired and thrilled for her, grateful that I was there to witness it. I remember the night sky, the netting and sound of the hardware clacking against the poles, the shouts of joy and encouragement and the smell of autumn in Texas.  This resets my mind and spirit. They had a program to inflict the west coast, namely the cities our president considers as collateral damage, namely, San Diego, Los Angeles and San Francisco. Then after the Japanese surrender, the general suggested suicide bombing missions in the same area. If it wasn’t for a prescient General Umezu who stopped it in its tracks because he said Japan would earn the ‘derision of the world’ and that humanity would then be fighting bacteria. This operation was called Operation Cherry Blossom. What is worse is Ishii was never held responsible for war crimes in China because the US wanted him forgiven so they could use him in our biowarfare program. 
Never did I think I would be more scared than a nuclear bomb scenario. But seriously what is wrong with the military in all countries? What is wrong with leadership that is unable to project unforeseen consequences of actions?

A day or two after it happened, I took the L across Manhattan and stood with others on the West Side Highway to cheer on the workers driving into the calamity. I was high on civic patriotism, and I was not the only one. So many dust-covered people coming off a ferry or walking into Brooklyn over the bridge. They basically turned our apartment living room into a lab collecting all kinds of samples. They told us then, 25 years ago, that the air and the dust was highly toxic and that we should not return to living in Battery Park City. My wife was even interviewed on the Today Show.  We never went back and sold our condo at a huge loss and threw out all of our furniture and toys. We loved BPC but at the time we were shamed for no being more supportive to the community.  -- It was pretty obvious, even without all of the testing that breathing this in everyday was really bad.

comments.name: Doug Terry
comments.body:
This morning the National Hurricane Center is projecting this hurricane will be at something close to, or just above, tropical storm strength when it moves onshore. The actual wind power, unless a storm is above Category Three, should not be a prime focus. Storm surge, which moves ocean water onto land as far as it is able to push it, is a source of greater danger to life than wind.

I am reporting on this storm, with the able assistance of the NY Times and other sources, at https://ernnews.com, as I have been doing through a non-profit effort for a number of years. (I am a veteran reporter/news manager.)

During the day yesterday, the Center, and its AI aided computers, projected that the storm would turn eastward as it moved upward across the south. Today, the projected line is straighter, more northward so the storm might spare the more eastern states from heavy rain.

One of the chief dangers of this storm is likely to be flooding, depending on how fast it moves northward. That means everyone in flood prone areas across the entire the projected path should move out of areas at the base of hills and mountains and anywhere flooding has occurred in the past (near creeks and rivers). If the storm's movement should stall out, flooding would become intense and very life threatening.

Look around your house and where you expect to ride out the storm. Tree branches, large and small, will likely fall, even some distance inland and whole trees could come down, posing great danger.

comments.body: Immense gratitude for my high school teachers who introduced me to Anne Carson. The Glass Essay was my bedtime story when I was 16. She is my constant inspiration in writing and in living.

comments.name: Elizabeth
comments.body:
I was thrilled to discover Anne Carson’s work as she was writing it, and so I feel an almost familial love for her and her work and a delight in her gorgeous mind. I am always just so proud of her! Although her erudition and brilliance gleams over all the pages of her work, she’s one of those amazing poet/thinker/writers who makes everyone I’ve ever taught want to pick up a pen and write too. She’s a particular kind of community bard who considers the work of composing all kinds of stuff to be honest labor; she knows her predilections and skills and interests so deeply and honestly and naturally that she makes the reader who wants to write realize that the first step in finding the real work is to get as excited as a child about knowing your own simple enthusiasms and curiosity, and starting there. In this, she inspires lots of us in the same manner that Jane Goodall did. If it’s chimpanzees you love, just do that. The rest will follow. That will make a lifetime of honest work for the good of us all. 

As she concludes in “God’s Work,” “…” you can see how much work remains to do./ Put away your sadness, it is a mantle of work.”

comments.name: eaa
comments.body: All good recommendations. I would add Carson's hilarious and profound poem "Pronoun Envy," first published in The New Yorker I think.  It's a witty takedown of binary thinking and of Harvard's Linguistics department, including its treatment of women graduate students in the early 1970s. Exhibits best Carson's rambunctious humor and sense of wonder, as well as the inspiration she drew from 1970s feminism's aesthetics of imitation, parody, and revision.

comments.name: Joshua Marie Wilkinson
comments.body: I found out this morning that she'd won when the poet Mathias Svalina texted me: ANNE CRSN NOBL PRIZ. I first encountered her work as an undergrad in Bruce Beasley's course in the late 90s. Once Anne called me when I was teaching a class. She was in town for a conference and wanted my help locating a swimming pool, which I had promised her, but unfortunately did not exist. I was standing in front of a class of my students when I answered my flip phone and apologized for the mistake about the pool, which was actually my lie to get her to come to the conference in Denver, where I was a grad student. Personal favorites of mine: Eros the Bittersweet, Decreation, Nox, Men in the Off Hours, Short Talks, and Autobiography of Red. I first saw Carson read several years earlier in 2000 in Seattle, with my mother. My mom died this past spring and I'm sorry I can't call her to share this news with her. Congratulations to Anne Carson.

This is a lovely story.  
Yes, Kartoffeln are certainly an irreplaceable part of the German diet and culture, and are also widely eaten all over Europe.  However Kartoffeln did not originate in Germany, or in Europe at all.  They originated in wild form in South America.

Tomaten, perhaps more a part of the typical Italian diet than German - are also widely eaten all over Europe.  Tomaten originated in the wild in South America too.

comments.body: There is more than a little bit of irony in the fact that a book about sleeping beauties explores a theme that was already written about quite elegantly in the book Sleeping Beauties, by evolutionary biologist Andreas Wagner (great read, by the way). If the topic interests you, check out Anthony van Raan's work in the field of scientonetrics. Ironic or not, I welcome Byrne's entry into a very fascinating realm of research,including much good empirical work across domains.

comments.name: Matt
comments.body:
Gives evidence against a conventional wisdom that  strongly discourages potentially useful innovations.
One is market place logic as in “Build a better mousetrap and the world will beat a path to your door.” 
Another is the assumption, even in the innovation-touting community, that we can even recognize those that don’t look like what we’re expecting.
As this book review shows, we miss things, even big things.
I see no sign that that knowledge has changed anything.
The tips given to speed things up are OK, but hardly sufficient to encourage and find the innovations we will need to help us meet our monster challenges.
And these innovations are not just technical, another misperception. They can be social.
I’m on my way right now to a rejuvenating the nuclear sector conference.
We’ll see if they’ve moved beyond historic business-as-usual thinking that created technical and communications problems that weren’t supposed to happen.

comments.name: Louis
comments.body:
This is a subject that has long interested me - perhaps in part because I work in marketing  - and I'm looking forward to reading Byrne's thoughts. I read that Moby Dick was unappreciated for decades before later being considered a classic. 

Sometimes this is due to changes in taste or understanding - like the example of atomic theory,a  work can truly be ahead of its time. 

Partially this is due to the probabalistic nature of our world: some ideas make it through while others randomly whither. With AI the number of new ideas will explode even faster than before. How many great ones will go unrealized?

comments.name: George Fleming
comments.body:
A. J. Liebling said "If man remembered everything he invented, there would be nothing left to invent."  I can't get enough of Liebling, and I know what he meant.  Never mind "man."  That was back in the day, let's give him a break.
  
But I demur.  There will be no end of new things.  The field is infinite.  I came up with some of it myself.  But in technical work "Not Invented Here" is no joke.  People believe that if they didn't think of it, it won't work.   I have a long list of quotes about it:

"The test of an invention is the power of an inventor to push it through in the face of staunch – not opposition, but indifference – in society."
– Edwin Land

"In the science, there is ego."   Katalin Karikó, Nobel Prize for mRNA

“It is a curious property of research activity that after the problem has been solved the solution seems obvious.”
– Edwin Land

comments.name: Howell
comments.body:
Democritus was an ancient Greek philosopher who theorized that matter could not be infinitely divisible. At a small enough scale, he concluded, any substance must be comprised of discrete "atoms" moving through an empty void--an astonishing leap of intuition.  

The idea was rejected by more influential figures of the time and largely forgotten. It would not be revisited for over two millennia when Enlightenment thinkers began to question the ancient orthodoxy. Finally, in 1808, the English chemist John Dalton provided the first experimental proof of the atomic theory of matter, vindicating Democritus 2,400 years after his death.

Talk about an idea that was ahead of its time!

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
The review does not distinguish between late-stage capitalism of the "Information Age," simulacra, and spectacle and early print culture of Vermeer, before Walter Benjamin's work of art "aura" dissipated in "the age of mechanical reproduction." Dissonant and unexplicated is the difference of scale between Vermeer's salvaging of reputation and that of twentieth-century Van Gogh, Joyce, Pound, etc. The modern is, in fact, peculiar to history--only a few centuries, at best, in the face of millennia going back to the Greeks. Perhaps the ambivalent individual identification of David Byrne as under-appreciated a few decades separated--as far as I can tell--from the inception of his Talking Heads commercial success is given cultural context by Timothy Murray's Theatrical Legitimation: Allegories of Genius in Seventeenth-Century France and England (1987). Primitive accumulation of capital began in 1550s England when the trope of resemblance prevailed rather than the episteme of binary opposition.

If Shakespeare sources the modern, he was underestimated, too, in his own lifetime. The self-effacing player-sharer of the most successful theater company took a backseat to Ben Jonson, considered the greater playwright, then.

She did so grudgingly but it worked and led her to long term sobriety.  And eventually to a conversion to Catholicism.  The reverse journey for many recovering folks raised as catholics. comments.name: Sean S.
comments.body:
I’m looking forward to reading this book. 

Like O’Gieblyn, I am sober for some time and also grapple with that deep longing that alcoholics carry inside, the “God shaped hole.” I have also attempted to fill it with a conception of God and church that itself is more of a false idol than a true connection. 

The place I’ve landed, thankfully without having a relapse, is that the longing is the connection and that living with the discomfort of being alive is the daily work. I do get meaning and release from deeper religious and spiritual practice, but when I treat it like an escape then I’m off track. 

As an old hippy I got sober with many years ago used to say, “Reality is an acquired taste.”

The late Pope Francis said wine was a gift of God.

Humans have always pondered the afterlife and religions filled that need.
Humans also have always wanted to alter their consciousness with different drugs.  Wine easily beat out the competition.  The Catholic church, answering both desires, is now the largest church on earth.  The priest's
robes are like Togas.

A grand mal seizure is violent and transforms its sufferer into someone unrecognizable.  We would still have to get up in the morning and go to school and try to make sense of the world. On our own. This filmmaker got to the core of this experience in a way that’s difficult to explain. Was it because the film was also so lyrical? That scene of the man and child in the ocean is etched in my mind. All I know is that I sat in the theater and sobbed for a long time at the end of the film.

Jack was devoted to the comic strip "Nancy", which puzzled me because I thought "Nancy" was garbage.  Now that I am older, I think we were both right. "Nancy" was awful in the 1970s, but in the 1940s through the early 1960s, it was brilliant. I think the decline started in the mid 1960s.

comments.name: Emile
comments.body:
I'm stunned that three's zero mention of Bushmiller's DRAWNG in this piece. Yes, Bushmiller was a writer with a gag, but he was also an artist.

Bushmiller gave Nancy a round face with cheeks that are round enough to stick out, minimalist eyebrows and eyes, a quick dark horizontal line for her nose, and an oval that can go up or down or turn into a lined grin with dimples. Plus there's her hair--that helmet made of solid black with spiky contours and a bow affised near the low brow. The other characters have their own specifics, but Nancy herself takes the prize.

Bushmiller worked out the drawing we now think of as Nancy only after a couple of years of constinually modifying her. For a great book on the evolution of Nancy try getting hold of the catalogue The Nancy Show, which accompanied the 2024 exhibition of the same name at the Billy Ireland Cartoon LIbrary and Museum at the Ohio State University in 2024. I hage been a lover of Nancy since I was a small child, and flew out there to see it.

comments.name: Liemba
comments.body:
Mr. Waller seems to contradict himself quite a bit in his speech, giving the impression that Fed officials are now trying desperately to backtrack on their decision after realizing the latest rate hike was a mistake.

First, without solid anticipation of a plausible trajectory of consistent future rate hikes, raising one-time or sporadic quarter-point rates will likely fail to signal the Fed’s strong commitment to anchoring inflation expectations. The only economic impact of such a hike will be to marginally raise costs for everyone without achieving any policy goals.

How many more consecutive hikes will the Fed be able to realistically afford to execute after the first one in the current economic environment, before it is forced to pause and reassess? It has no option but to raise rates again to maintain its posturing. However, now it appears that the Fed is already likely to pause after the very first hike.

Second, his speech makes it sound like the Fed may have raised rates in an attempt to preemptively combat inflation, even though the concern was moderate inflationary pressure rather than severe, double-digit inflation. Reacting sensitively to every small percentage tick in inflation data could erode public confidence and trust in the Fed and the economy.

In my view, the Fed has just cornered itself with its rushed decision to prematurely hike rates. In the end, things will likely only get a little more expensive for everyone without yielding any tangible benefits.

BTW, the Lauren bug is an example of something all software with the potential for this sort of failure should be protected against.  One of the things I learned in class was in data entry code you need to protect against things like users pressing two keys simultaneously.  No matter how skilled and experienced they are humans make mistakes.

comments.name: Phil
comments.body: Her invaluable contribution to the Apollo programs was that she not only wrote software, she also made the software robust.  That means it could handle an operator pushing the wrong button, or the computer becoming overwhelmed with input, without blowing up and failing.  That was absolutely critical in Apollo 11's descent to the lunar surface.  Without that robust code, the landing would likely have had to abort.

comments.name: Down Home Doctor
comments.body: I admire her persistence and discipline in a hostile environment.  My late sister, we were told some years after her death, is known as "the grandmother of the internet" but searching for her work in database development and her other fields on said internet yields no results.  So, we are left to wonder.  All I know is that I'd ask her every holiday to explain to me once again what she did for a living and still not quite get it.  I'd invented a code in BASIC for an actually random shuffle of cards in the early 80's in the Harvard extension school, but my male instructors took the patent, and I headed off into another challenging sort of career at another Ivy.  So, whatever she was doing, it was flying right over the heads of a roomful of similarly focused people with brains that registered well with standardized testing -- hardly the only valid way to measure intelligence, I hasten to say! In fact, (having written questions for some of them) I find those tests and our reliance on them to be rather foolish since they only capture a narrow population of a narrow range of types of intelligence.  Engineers do love their competitions and ranking of difficulty and utility, but they also often aren't all that good at thinking outside a box, any box. Just waiting for the day when "neurodivergence" is an obsolete word and instead a point on a spectrum of a fuller understanding of what "intelligence" is considered normal, far beyond what any test can capture at this point.

comments.name: GvN
comments.body:
What the article omitted is that Margaret's programming was so tedious because it was done in assembly code. Assembly is just barely a step up from programming in binary and requires an intimate knowledge of the hardware on which your programs are running. THAT and Margaret's meticulous coding is why it worked!
Nowadays anyone can write computer programs and have the compiler turn it into the zeros and ones, no need to know what you are trying to program. As a result programs have become bloated and slow. The only saving grace is increasingly faster hardware, enormous memory capacity, better compilers and now AI (sorry SI :\) to write the programs for you.

comments.name: Joshua Kline
comments.body:
Laos has decided to rely on Chinese aid to address its deplorable infrastructure and technological deficiencies, just as other countries rely on the US, Japan, and Europe for the same.   Its electrical grid and transportation system were pathetic, and now a country that never had a railroad has a higher-quality north-south line that runs faster than many in the US. Freight and people can now move as never before—the "before" being an awful dirt two-track line that I traveled several times.  It was so bad that, in one case, several people left the bus, too road-sick to continue.

To claim that the RR "largely bypasses the local population" is false.  Anybody can buy a ticket, and when I rode the line from Vientiane to the Chinese border, the train was packed, largely with Laotians boarding and deboarding at Lao stations along the way. 
   Indebtedness is a problem and a decision for every nation, and the percentage of Laos's GDP owed to China is indeed huge.  But that is between China and Laos. Laos's reliance on China is offset by vast improvements.  The US could have offered similar assistance at any time, instead it dropped bombs.

 From 1964 to 1973, the US conducted roughly 580,000 bombing missions over Laos and dropped over 2 million tons of ordnance (figures from the US government and International sources). These included cluster bombs, 80 million of which failed to explode and continue to kill and wound people today.  I prefer China's contribution.

Decades after visiting an ex-Jesuit priest who lived as a companion and help-mate to a a Steinbeck curator, in a house once belonging to John Steinbeck in Pacific Grove, California, I asked both of the experts on Steinbeck (ex-priest also guide in Cannery Row) why there was no prequel to "East of Eden" that addressed the sociopathic schizophrenic Cathy, the way that Jean Rhys addressed the backdrop of what created Jane Eyre's Bertha, the mad woman in the attic. After all, the copyright statute of limitation had elapsed. Their response is not addressed here.

Recently I have seen such a depiction on Netflix, which gives a background story to Cathy who cannot return the warmth that Adam Trask feels for her, or for anyone else, but feels a kinship with his mischievous, rule-breaking brother Charles Trask. 

Recognition is the closest she gets to love. When Charles disappears from her schizophrenic reverie (she hears his voice) it serves as a first step to embracing herself. (spoiler alert!) 

Whilst opening a closed door, with the assistance of Morpheus, she sees her 5 year-old self crawling out from a furnace, coming out of the dark hole that early childhood rape inflicted upon her. She sinks into eternal sleep, forgetfulness.

It was well-done for a TV show. But depicting Cathy as a monster  misses the monsters who preyed upon her once vulnerable self, before the armour sheltered her from further anguish.

Unstable governments are a common feature of proportional rep voting systems. The fringe parties also hold the balance of power and have disproportionate influence. In most countries the majority are centrist - leaning slightly left and right. Proportional rep does not serve the majority well.

First-past-the post is a much better system that generally forms more stable governments where fringe parties have little influence. That is a good thing. The exception is where regional parties come into play - but that problem exists with proportional rep as well.

Nebulous Decision Boundaries in the Age of AI

When deep neural networks encounter out-of-distribution inputs, their feature representations often settle into nebulous clusters within the high-dimensional latent space, causing standard softmax calibrations to yield overconfident yet spurious predictions. To counter this ambiguity, researchers rely on uncertainty estimation techniques like Monte Carlo dropout and conformal prediction to clearly demarcate where the model's confidence ends.

comments.name: Joe Pearce
comments.body:
I have no real thoughts on this, since I enjoy this type of dancing and despite its increasing popularity over my lifetime, this opera can use a bit more life than parts of it have. 

But since we finally again have a Comments section for the new opera season, and there wasn't one for the MACBETH opening night review by Ousamma Zahr (spelling?), I would like to say here what I would have said then. Ms. Zahr's was absolutely the best review of an opera, at the Met or elsewhere, that I have seen in The Times in a good 20 years. 
For almost the only time in my immediate recollection, she wrote about what reviewers used to always write about - the opera, of course, the production, of course, and at great length, the singers (almost of course not, except for a couple of prior Davidsen debut roles, and then those reviews were always on the always-hyped Davidsen, and not for anyone else appearing on the stage with her). It's still here, so if you are an opera lover and haven't read it, by all means go to it now. It's the kind of opera review we haven't never seen from Messrs. Taommasini, Woolfe or Barone, and that, indeed, we might have to go all the way back to Crutchfield to last encounter. Bravo, Zahr!

But isn't it amazing that no commentary space was provided for that very important and overwhelmingly excellent opening night performance, while all of this space (much of it deserved) covers only the dancers in that same VOCAL work?

Somebody should pay attention to thse things!

comments.body: No worry.  We will continue to see problems caused by misuse of AI.  But AI's benefits will be far exceed any potential problems. Stop fear mongering. The same situation has played out for guns, which occasionally cause problems.  But guns are essential to defending our freedom and necessary to the security of a free State.

comments.name: SA
comments.body:
Stephen Witt penned an essay for the Times yesterday where he wondered if Jensen Huang's "Don't Worry, Be Happy" theory of AI might be slightly flawed.  He wondered what we commenters thought.  So, part of my response was this:

"Here is the problem, Stephen: I worry that one day I will wake up, check my bank accounts and my credit cards, and find that some 'bad actor' has used AI to make my accounts non-existent."

And so it begins!  The attempt may have been largely ineffective...but it's early times.

I don't see the future of AI as being particularly rosy.  Humans are not inherently stable creatures who just want to make the world a better place.  Many want mayhem and destruction whether they personally profit from it or not.

AI gives the evil geniuses out there exactly the tool they need.  

Pandora's Box has been opened.
